articles.title: The social ecology of trustworthiness inferences: Cultural gradients in emotion overgeneralization
articles.authors: Yuqing Shi; Ryutaro Uchiyama; Shuxian Jin; Yin Wang; Steve M. J. Janssen; Daniel DongWon Oh
articles.abstract: Judgments of trustworthiness from faces guide critical social decisions. It remains debated whether these judgments reflect shared features of human perception or are shaped by cultural experience. One prominent explanation is emotion overgeneralization: faces that structurally resemble emotional expressions elicit corresponding impressions, even when no emotion is displayed. Although often treated as universal, emotion overgeneralization may reflect ecological learning shaped by culture-specific norms. We propose a cultural gradient: where emotional expressions are more informative, the link between happiness resemblance and perceived trustworthiness should be stronger. Participants from 32 countries (N ≈ 6,400) will evaluate the trustworthiness of unfamiliar individuals from standardized resting facial photographs and complete a measure of emotional expressivity, with each face’s resemblance to happiness quantified computationally. We will test whether emotional expressivity is associated with greater emotion overgeneralization at both country and individual levels. Null results would favor perceptual invariance, whereas positive associations would support ecological calibration.

articles.title: Tracking vocabulary development as children start school: assessing measurement invariance in multilingual classrooms
articles.authors: Sonali Nag; Athina Ntalli; Gideon Arulmani; Joshua Aaron McGrane
articles.abstract: Receptive vocabulary, what is understood when hearing a word, underpins reading comprehension and wider learning. Yet, few tests have been validated to function fairly over developmental time and across diverse linguistic experiences. This study examined the Picture Test for Receptive Vocabulary (TalkTogether – Hindi), a 50-item test for four-to-nine-year-olds in multilingual north India. Words in the language of school instruction and linked images were drawn picture- and story books. Over one academic year (2023–2024), 1,949 administrations were collected from children (47% girls) at three time points across 40 schools. The test showed good reliability (Cronbach’s α = .82; Rasch reliability = .78) and captured variation across the proficiency range. Item properties remained stable across time, licensing its use as a fair tracking tool. Between-group differential item functioning (DIF) effects—by sex, home language(s), and a novel index of ambient peer language exposure—were small to negligible. The findings demonstrate that a contextually-situated vocabulary test, validated through rigorous psychometric evaluation, can meet the standards required for fair tracking of oral skills in the language of instruction. The reported protocol to inform item revision and evaluate dimensions of measurement invariance—demographic, contextual and developmental—are likely transferable to other similarly multilingual settings.

articles.title: An introduction to longitudinal multilevel and structural equation modeling approaches for examining change
articles.authors: Razieh Pourafshari; Miriam Brinberg; Joseph Bayer
articles.abstract: This chapter provides a practical introduction to two statistical frameworks for analyzing longitudinal data in quantitative communication research: multilevel modeling (MLM) and structural equation modeling (SEM). Focusing on intraindividual change and intraindividual variability, we illustrate how these methods can disentangle within-person processes from between-person differences. Using real-world data, the chapter demonstrates how to model daily patterns in social interaction desires and test dynamic relationships between social app use and interpersonal needs. Key considerations for choosing between MLM and SEM are discussed. The chapter also highlights advanced extensions, including nonlinear growth, mediation, and multivariate models, offering researchers a foundational guide for applying these approaches to their own questions examining change.

articles.title: From transdiagnostic compulsivity to clinical applications: a computational psychiatry approach to bridge research and clinic
articles.authors: Sean E Cavanagh; Toby Wise
articles.abstract: Compulsivity, the maladaptive persistence of behaviour despite adverse consequences, is central to obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and has been increasingly conceptualised as a transdiagnostic dimension spanning multiple neuropsychiatric disorders. Research within computational psychiatry has linked dimensional compulsivity to two candidate mechanisms: impaired goal-directed control and elevated metacognitive confidence. Here, we take a clinical perspective addressing how insights from these findings can be brought into practice. We first ask how dimensional compulsivity measures should be interpreted with respect to clinical presentations and discuss conflicts between the general population findings and clinical data. We highlight several challenges facing clinical implementation: effect sizes are small, goal-directed control has not been shown to change with either pharmacotherapy or psychological therapy, and the overconfidence associated with dimensional compulsivity contrasts with the reduced confidence reported in patients with OCD. We argue these discrepancies are informative rather than disqualifying and set out a translational roadmap for mechanistically informed detection and transdiagnostic intervention. Specifically, we suggest that screening and digital monitoring of dimensional compulsivity, combined with cognitive and mechanistic phenotyping to guide psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy, may ultimately improve outcomes across diagnostic boundaries.

articles.title: Multilingualism WithOut Words: A non-lexicalist model of bilingualism
articles.authors: Alexandra Krauska; Danielle Fahey
articles.abstract: Standard models of bilingualism are primarily concerned with how words in multiple languages are stored and associated in the mind. However, there is growing consensus in linguistic theory that language cannot be organized around words, given that meaning, syntax, and form do not always align at the word level. We propose the Multilingualism WithOut Words (M-WOW) model to realign models of bilingualism with current linguistic theory and account for a broader typology of languages. In contrast to other models, M-WOW allows more flexibility in how features are realized across languages and expands the possibilities for code-switching. Because the model does not rely on a word level, it accommodates a broader set of linguistic phenomena and provides new insights into bilingual language processing and the dynamic and variable processes of L2 acquisition and attrition.

articles.title: Noun memory advantage drives sentence internal primacy and recency at clause boundaries
articles.authors: Sebastián Mancha; Ellen Lau
articles.abstract: Classic research in psychology has shown that comprehenders in recall tasks ‘chunk’ word lists in order to facilitate later retrieval. Here we ask how chunking mechanisms apply in grammatically structured sentence stimuli. How do comprehenders make use of this grammatical structure to guide chunking of a sentence’s component words in memory? In previous studies of multi-clause sentence recall, many researchers have argued that chunking is clause-based, as evidenced by scalloped serial accuracy curves in which primacy and recency effects are observed within each clause. Here we suggest that these previous findings may have been driven by the correlation of sentence boundaries with nouns, a lexical class known to demonstrate an independent accuracy advantage in recall. Using immediate serial recall of naturalistic biclausal English sentences and manipulating noun placement, we find evidence that nouns indeed confer a large accuracy boost at the internal clause boundary that can explain prior results. We discuss the difficulty of applying serial position logic to highly structured representations such as those that underlie sentence forms.

articles.title: Not passive sponges: When attention wanes, our brains are less synchronized with the environment
articles.authors: Elena Greatti; Laura Batterink; Davide Crepaldi; Amy Finn
articles.abstract: Without even being aware, humans are amazingly sensitive to the structures around them. Is this sensitivity constant or does it fluctuate along with our attentional states? To answer this foundational question, we deployed temporally sensitive measures that allow us to track neural entrainment—the synchronization of brain activity to environmental regularities—alongside fluctuations in attentional states. Participants (n = 78) viewed both random and structured visual streams while performing a task to index fluctuating attentional states. Structured streams evoked robust neural entrainment and reduced attentional lapses. Moreover, attentional states varied with neural entrainment. Across participants, those who displayed greater neural entrainment had reduced attentional lapses. And critically, even within individuals, greater entrainment was observed during periods of greater attentional focus. Our sensitivity to structure and attentional states are therefore inextricably linked: structures stabilize our attentional states and our sensitivity to structure dynamically mirrors the ebb and flow of human attention.

articles.title: Machines in the Middle: How AI Use Changes What Coworkers Think of, and Do for, One Another
articles.authors: Maxine Parker; Celine Huang; Sekoul Krastev
articles.abstract: Generative AI is now embedded in how coworkers, leaders, and organizations communicate, yet its effects on the relationships among them are still poorly understood. This review synthesizes recent research on how an individual’s AI use changes the way others perceive, judge, and behave toward them, and shows that these effects can be explained by established theories of human-human interaction, including attribution theory, computers-as-social-actors, the integrative model of organizational trust, social exchange theory, and resource-based theories. The evidence suggests that observers often read AI use as a sign of disposition rather than circumstance, judging AI users as less competent, motivated, warm, and authentic, and that disclosure does not repair the resulting loss of trust. These perceptions carry over into behavior: coworkers reciprocate less, share less knowledge, and show less prosocial behavior toward AI users, while AI-related job insecurity, loneliness, and work alienation further strain ties among colleagues. AI use also loosens moral standards and shifts how blame is assigned, making people more critical of others’ work but more lenient toward misconduct. These effects are conditional rather than uniformly negative. AI can reduce loneliness, improve coordination, and prompt employees to invest more in emotionally supportive ties, and relational buffers such as leader-member exchange, shared leadership, and supervisor support can offset its costs. The review concludes that AI’s costs to workplace relationships run mainly through indirect pathways, not through the technology itself. It outlines organizational implications, including clear norms for when and why AI is used and protection of socially valued tasks, and identifies priorities for future research: longitudinal designs, team- and network-level studies, intervention research, and more diverse samples.

articles.title: Humans adaptively delay planning using cognitive maps
articles.authors: Paul B. Sharp; Eran Eldar
articles.abstract: Planning is an expensive computational operation that easily exhausts our cognitive resources. For this reason, it is critical to learn strategies to initiate planning wisely. To understand how humans adaptively initiate planning, we developed a task where humans can learn to delay planning at certain timepoints when all actions are equally likely to reach an instructed goal. Across two pre-registered studies, we show that humans adaptively delay planning, and improve in their ability to do so with experience. To explain this behavior, we formalize a model of the underlying meta-control computations. Our model demonstrates how strategies to delay planning are not learned from experienced outcomes, but rather, from searching a cognitive map of the task to determine at which points it is more valuable to delay control. We thus establish that humans can adaptively delay planning, and learn to do so by means of a cognitive map.

articles.title: Minds Meet Machines: The Joint Role of Trust and Intellectual Humility in AI Persuasion
articles.authors: Devora Newman; Almog Simchon; Ruth Mayo
articles.abstract: Research shows that AI models have a remarkable ability to change people’s minds following a short conversation, a notoriously difficult task for human communicators. Such persuasive paradigms provide a unique opportunity to examine which psychological characteristics predict receptivity to counter-attitudinal information. We focus on two characteristics: intellectual humility (IH), reflecting openness to revising one’s beliefs following new information, and trust in the information source (AI). To establish the role of a-priori dispositions that determine acceptance of new information, we ran two online studies, sampling British participants with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants (N = 294). We replicated previous findings showing significant and lasting attitude change following a brief exchange with GPT, but crucially, this effect was not uniform. In Study 1, attitude change was greatest among participants with higher initial trust in AIs and higher intellectual humility. Study 2 extended this finding by measuring both dispositions a week before the conversation with GPT, revealing the same pattern: opinion change was greatest among those who were both open to new information and trusting of its source. These findings highlight the centrality of recipient dispositions, suggesting that the relationship between source trust and persuasion depends on recipients' intellectual humility. More broadly, source trust may function as more than a heuristic cue, and its relationship with attitude change may depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the fallibility of their beliefs. Together, these findings extend perspectives on persuasion by highlighting the joint role of source trust and recipients' epistemic dispositions in belief revision.

articles.title: Celebrity Endorsement and Meditation Intention: A Randomized Experiment
articles.authors: Michael Bowen
articles.abstract: Meditation offers well-documented health benefits, yet persistence with meditation is low. Drawing on the Reasoned Action Approach, we tested whether celebrity meditators as a descriptive-norm cue improve attitudes toward and intention to meditate. In this randomized survey experiment (N = 2,035), participants viewed one of four images captioned "Meditating for just a few minutes a day can transform your mind". Compared to same-gender non-celebrities, the celebrity images did not increase intention to meditate (female: OR = 0.88, 95% CI 0.64–1.21; male: OR = 1.18, 0.85–1.63) or change attitudes (female: b = −0.09, −0.19 to 0.00; male: b = 0.06, −0.03 to 0.14; all Holm-adjusted p ≥ .24). In conclusion, a single exposure to a celebrity meditator may be insufficient to shift attitudes or intentions toward meditation.

articles.title: Gamblers' behavior in a self-exclusion system with social barriers to revocation: evidence from Chile
articles.authors: Omar D. Perez; José Rafael Arenas Rojas; Mario Sanclemente Villegas; Steve Sharman
articles.abstract:
Background and aims: In most self-exclusion programs, leaving is the gambler's own decision. In Chile, by contrast, revocation requires the consent of a sponsor whom the participant nominates at enrollment and may later replace. We investigated whether the relationship with the first sponsor, and later changes of sponsor, relate to how long participants remain excluded.

Methods: We analyzed records from Chile's self-exclusion registry (2019–2025; N = 3,825 participants; 1,753 revocations). Time to first revocation was examined using Kaplan–Meier curves and time-varying Cox models including the relationship with the first sponsor, the direction of replacements, and prior rejected requests, accounting for the three-month waiting period after a replacement.

Results: Participants whose first sponsor was a close family member had a lower revocation hazard than those who nominated a partner (HR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.59–0.76); their median time to revocation was 40.4 months, against 20 to 22 months in the other groups. More importantly, replacing a non-family sponsor with a close family member was followed by a lower hazard (HR = 0.59), whereas the reverse change showed no detectable difference. Each rejected request, and each replacement once the waiting period had ended, was associated with a higher hazard, with many revocations right after that period.

Discussion and conclusions: Having a close family member as sponsor, whether from enrollment or after a replacement, is associated with longer exclusions. These results are discussed in the light of the sponsor's role as a social commitment device and the points at which participants may benefit from support.

articles.title: Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks
articles.authors: Gaël Carniel; Valentin Guigon; Frédéric Moisan; Alain Barrat; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments. We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy. Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates. During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden. Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection. Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources. Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure. Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Altered pre-supplementary motor area recruitment during semantic inhibition in individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits
articles.authors: Rebeca Villarroel; Francisco Marcano; José Luis González-Mora; Manuel de Vega; Iván Padrón González; Mariano Díaz-Rivera; Damián Jan; Cristián Modroño
articles.abstract:
Background: Inhibitory control dysfunction has been implicated in obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), but neuroimaging research has focused predominantly on motor response inhibition. Whether obsessive–compulsive traits are associated with altered neural recruitment during semantic inhibition remains unclear.
Methods: Forty right-handed participants with lower or elevated obsessive–compulsive traits performed an fMRI adaptation of the Hayling Sentence Completion Task. Participants either selected an expected sentence completion (initiation) or suppressed this strongly prepotent response to select an unrelated word (inhibition). Whole-brain and anatomically defined region-of-interest (ROI) analyses examined task-related activation and Group × Condition interactions, with particular interest in the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) and SMA proper.
Results: Semantic inhibition produced a robust behavioural cost in reaction times and error rates, with no significant differences between groups. Whole-brain analysis identified the strongest inhibition-related activation in the left preSMA. The exploratory Group × Condition analysis also yielded its peak interaction in this region. Anatomically defined ROI analysis showed a significant Group × Condition interaction in the preSMA after family-wise error correction (t = 2.56, pFWE = .012), reflecting a larger inhibition-related increase in controls compared to individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits. The corresponding interaction in SMA proper did not reach statistical significance (t = 1.74, pFWE = .084).
Conclusions: Elevated obsessive–compulsive traits were associated with altered preSMA recruitment during semantic inhibition in absence of behavioural impairment. This extends neural markers of obsessive–compulsive alterations from the domain of motor inhibition to that of semantic inhibition.

articles.title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for cognitive rehabilitation
articles.authors: Jamie Berry; Marc L. Copersino
articles.abstract:
This chapter describes a neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) approach to
cognitive rehabilitation (CR) following acquired brain injury (ABI), with primary
emphasis on traumatic brain injury and stroke. NIPE is conceptualised as more than
information provision: neuroscience-informed explanations are used to help patients
and families understand cognitive difficulties, recovery, rehabilitation strategies, and
their implications for everyday functioning. Neuropsychological feedback is presented
as a common context for NIPE, with attention to tailoring, functional translation,
multimodal support, and verification of understanding.
A dual-lens framework is proposed for NIPE delivery in CR. The therapeutic lens
emphasises alliance, empathy and warmth, person-centred collaboration, shared
explanatory models, and goal setting. The cognition-informed lens addresses how
cognitive difficulties may affect learning through adjustment of information load and
pacing, repetition, clear and concrete language, integration with existing knowledge,
teach-back, and multimodal delivery. Together, these lenses inform considerations of
timing and context and seven structural principles of NIPE: trustworthiness, interaction,
salience, motivation, intensity, repetition, and multimodal/multimedia delivery.
The chapter also considers NIPE content related to neuroplasticity, prognosis and
recovery, rehabilitation approaches, and factors that may influence functioning and
participation. Throughout, emphasis is placed on distinguishing established evidence
from plausible but untested mechanisms and on presenting recovery in probabilistic
rather than deterministic terms.

articles.title: Comment on Suresh et al. (2026): Drug-level sample size, validation and embedding confounds in receptor–semantic mappings
articles.authors: Tim Kmecl
articles.abstract: Suresh et al. (2026, Psychopharmacology) related GloVe embeddings of 4,496 first-hand reports of 21 psychedelic drugs to receptor affinity profiles using partial least squares regression (PLSR), and reported associations between specific receptors and experiential themes. Because affinities vary only between drugs, every report of a drug carries the same profile. I show algebraically that within-drug variation drops out of every cross-product with the affinities. The published loadings can be reproduced from the drug means alone (r ≥ 0.998), so the analysis rests on 21 drugs, with a Kish effective sample size of about 11, rather than on 4,496 reports. The model is near-saturated at the drug level. The cross-validation, receptor subset selection and loading interpretation have not been assessed at the drug level, and the associations have not been tested against chance or for generalisation beyond the few heavily weighted drugs, within the sample or to new ones. A reanalysis of published values shows that the first three components closely follow the DMT–MDMA contrast (r = 0.93), mean report length (r = 0.96) and the LSD–DMT contrast (r = 0.97). The length component follows from summing word vectors. I propose drug-level validation, permutation and resampling analyses that can be run on the existing data. Code reproducing all numbers is publicly available.

articles.title: Connected or drained? An experience sampling study on informal communication and well-being in hybrid work settings
articles.authors: Alicia Andrea Meier-Ernst; Leonard Reinecke
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Informal communication has been ascribed well-being functions. Yet in increasingly hybrid work settings, where employees work remotely, informal exchanges frequently occur via digital channels and may hinder relational bonds and drain rather than restore employees’ energy. Drawing on Communicate Bond Belong Theory, this study examines whether informal communication enhances or undermines employees’ well-being in hybrid settings by considering its perceived quality, relational benefits, and energy-related costs. Design/methodology/approach: A one-week experience sampling study (26 participants; 549 surveys) captured employees’ everyday communication episodes with co-workers and their subsequent experiences. Mixed-effects models estimated within-person relationships while accounting for between-person differences.
Findings: Episodes that were more informal than usual were associated with higher striving potential (e.g., more pleasantness or meaningfulness). In turn, higher striving potential was associated with more relatedness need satisfaction and a more favorable relatedness-to-energy ratio, though not with energy expenditure. Communication modality did not moderate these associations. However, text-based (vs. audio-visual) exchanges were significantly associated with lower relatedness and energy expenditure, and a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio. Originality: Adopting a situational perspective, this study moves beyond frequency-based and between-person approaches to everyday informal communication. It disentangles message- and channel-related effects and their distinct contributions in the relationship between informal talk and employee well-being. From this novel perspective, the findings provide evidence that informal communication is a resource for employees’ well-being, but can impose demands when it occurs digitally, an aspect that practitioners should recognize when designing informal communication initiatives.

articles.title: Trusting the Machine: Separating Trust in GenAI Authors from Trust in Their Content
articles.authors: Caroline Simpson; Clara Colombatto; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang
articles.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes more sophisticated and widespread, it matters how its perceived humanness affects trust. Previous work shows that anthropomorphism increases an agent’s perceived trustworthiness as an advisor. We asked whether an author’s presentation also affects trust in the information it produces in a non-advisory role. In two experiments, participants read a science communication blog post attributed to an author with varying anthropomorphic cues. They rated the trustworthiness of the author (author trust) and the content (content trust). In Experiment 1 (N = 270), the post was attributed to a GenAI author described with low or high anthropomorphic cues, or to a human expert. The human author, who also differed in implied professional expertise, received higher author trust than either GenAI author. This effect was reliably larger than the effect on content trust. The low- and high-cue GenAI authors did not reliably differ, including in anthropomorphism ratings. In Experiment 2 (N = 148, preregistered), participants chatted with a GenAI chatbot, presented as the author, that used fewer (low condition) or more (high condition) anthropomorphic cues. The high-cue chatbot was rated more anthropomorphic and received modestly higher author trust. No reliable content trust effect was detected, and evidence that the two effects differed was inconclusive. Author and content trust were strongly correlated in both experiments. These results suggest that cues to an author’s humanness may shape trust in the author more than in what it communicates, although the clearest evidence came from comparing human and GenAI authors.

articles.title: Seeing a partner’s gestures in conversation increases referential but not form alignment: Evidence for distinct mechanisms of alignment in co-speech gestures
articles.authors: Sho Akamine; antje meyer; Asli Ozyurek
articles.abstract: People often align with one another’s sentence structures, lexical choices, and co-speech gestures during conversation. Such linguistic alignment has been attributed to both low-level priming and high-level collaborative efforts to establish mutual understanding (grounding). Although the contributions of these processes have been extensively investigated for verbal aspects of language use, their roles in co-speech gestural alignment remain largely unexplored. Here, we manipulated partner visibility in a video-mediated dyadic referential communication game (n = 45 dyads) to examine (i) whether priming and grounding contribute to the two dimensions of gestural alignment: referential and form alignment, and (ii) how lexical alignment relates to gestural alignment. We found that participants produced referentially aligned gestures more frequently when they could see their partner’s gestures than when they could not, irrespective of whether their own gestures were visible to their partner. This pattern provides evidence consistent with priming, but not with the predicted grounding effect. By contrast, visibility had little to no effect on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)-based gesture form similarity, suggesting that the contributions of priming and grounding may differ between referential and form alignment. Furthermore, lexical alignment was positively associated with the frequency of referentially aligned gestures, even after accounting for control variables. This association is consistent with the possibility that shared conceptualization of referents contributes to gestural alignment. Taken together, these findings highlight that mechanisms underlying alignment may differ depending on the dimensions of gestural alignment and point to distinct roles for priming and shared conceptualization in the alignment of co-speech gestures.

articles.title: iOS Shortcuts as a Free, No-Code Tool for Event-Triggered Experience Sampling
articles.authors: Douglas A. Parry; Tilo Hartmann
articles.abstract: Event-triggered experience sampling prompts in situ surveys when specific behaviors or contexts occur. This approach is valuable for capturing infrequent or context-bound experiences but often requires custom or expensive software. This article describes how iOS Shortcuts, a pre-installed automation feature, can provide a free, no-code alternative for event-triggered surveys on iPhones. Using trigger-action programming, researchers can configure automations that launch survey URLs with embedded contextual parameters when designated events occur. We describe the procedure, outline a workflow of triggers, actions, and embedded variables, and illustrate the approach with worked examples and templates.

articles.title: Cognitive performance in young and middle-aged adults with obesity: a systematic literature review
articles.authors: Camille Sellier; Marie-Claude Brindisi; Léopold Fezeu; Cecilia Samieri; Valentina A. Andreeva; Stéphanie Chambaron
articles.abstract:
Objective
This systematic review synthesizes prospective evidence on associations between obesity assessed in young or middle adulthood and subsequent cognitive performance before age 65.
Methods
A comprehensive search of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Web of Science identified prospective studies comparing adults with obesity to those of normal weight and assessing cognitive performance, using validated cognitive tests. Risk of bias was evaluated using ROBINS-E, and findings were synthesized narratively.
Results
Among 4,871 records screened, four publications representing three cohorts met the inclusion criteria. Two publications from Whitehall II reported small negative associations between obesity assessed in adulthood and global cognitive performance, whereas the MIDUS analysis found no longitudinal association for BMI. A modestly steeper 10-year decline in global cognition was reported among metabolically unhealthy adults with obesity compared with adults of normal weight in Whitehall II. Findings for executive function and memory were inconsistent and generally small. One study was judged at high risk of bias and the other three raised some concerns.
Conclusions
The available evidence is too sparse, heterogeneous, and methodologically uncertain to establish a meaningful independent association between obesity and cognitive performance before age 65. Future prospective studies should include cognitive assessment at baseline and repeated follow-up, report standardized effect estimates, use domain-specific cognitive outcomes, address confounding a priori, and assess central adiposity and metabolic health alongside BMI, particularly in younger adults.
PROSPERO registration: CRD42024573250
Keywords: Adults, Cognitive functions, Cohort studies, Executive functions, Obesity

articles.title: Tales of Life: Curiosity for Positive and Negative Life Stories of Culturally Close and Distant Others
articles.authors: Esther Niehoff; Marret Noordewier; Malgorzata A Goclowska; Suzanne Oosterwijk
articles.abstract: Personalized stories about others’ life experiences are omnipresent in media, yet we know little about what drives people to engage with such narratives. Across two studies (N = 596 UK adults), we investigated how valence (positive versus negative life event) and cultural distance (experience from someone from a culturally close versus distant country) shape social curiosity. Consistently, participants reported greater curiosity for stories about negative life events, especially when the story’s protagonist was culturally close. Structural equation modelling revealed that the relationship between negative valence and higher curiosity was mediated through greater anticipated insight and – counterintuitive at first sight – greater anticipated distress towards negative stories. At the same time, curiosity for negative stories was attenuated through lower expected enjoyment. These findings suggest that curiosity is driven by anticipated emotional impact of either valence, and have implications for fostering empathy and meaningful engagement in media and public discourse.

articles.title: Bayesian Treed Regressions for Estimating Heterogeneous Trajectories of Test Scores in Large-scale Educational Assessments
articles.authors: Mingya Huang
articles.abstract: In large-scale educational assessment, students’ academic outcomes can evolve over time, due to various effect modifiers. For instance, parents’  education level, a common modifier, has been found to have time-varying effects on children’s test scores, leading to heterogeneous academic trajectories. To model these varying trajectories, parametric models like hierarchical linear models (HLMs) are commonly deployed. While these highly parametric methods are interpretable, their predictive capacities have not been rigorously compared to those of more flexible nonparametric approaches. We present the results of systematic simulation studies and empirical analyses comparing traditional parametric models to Bayesian nonparametric models based on Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART). Our findings indicate that BART-based alternatives can (1) achieve comparable out-of-sample prediction as HLMs, after accounting for individual variability over time; (2) provide a reasonable amount of interpretability and uncertainty quantification; and (3) do not incur much more computational burden. This work contributes to the existing social science literature by demonstrating that Bayesian treed regression methods are viable and feasible alternatives to conventional HLMs for predicting heterogeneous trajectories across time.

articles.title: Age-related underestimation of smartphone screen time
articles.authors: Wenyu Wan; Maria G. Jol; Arko Ghosh
articles.abstract: There is growing evidence that self-reported media use poorly reflects real use, yet self-reports remain the dominant method in media research. Furthermore, the capacity to self-regulate smartphone use intuitively depends on how accurately one perceives that use. Here, we directly compared self-reported and objectively logged smartphone screen time in 304 participants aged 20 to 84 years. We found that reporting bias was strongly age-dependent: older adults underestimated their use while younger adults overestimated theirs. The age-related reporting bias was not explained by working memory performance (2-back task). Working memory did not mediate the association between age and reporting discrepancy. Our findings indicate that self-reported smartphone use carry little information on real use. We highlight the importance of objective measures of smartphone use and the need for understanding mechanisms which distort perceived use.

articles.title: From use perception to use behavior: Digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being in daily life
articles.authors: Krisna Adiasto; Fenne große Deters; Lisanne Sarah Pauw; Katharina Salo; Anne Milek
articles.abstract: Research on smartphone use and psychological well-being has yielded ambivalent and generally small effects. Three methodological limitations contribute to this inconsistency: studies typically capture smartphone use through aggregate measures such as screen time, rely on self-reported estimates that are systematically biased, and focus predominantly on between-person differences while neglecting within-person dynamics. The present study addresses these limitations by examining the between- and within-person associations between digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being. Using device logged app use data from a 10-day ecological momentary assessment study of romantic couples (N = 342 individuals), we examined five smartphone use purposes – active social use, passive social use, news consumption, entertainment, and practical use – in relation to positive affect, negative affect, and perceived stress. Analyses were replicated across two subsets to circumvent the dyadic structure of the data, and as an internal robustness check. Across both subsets, associations between digitally traced use purposes and well-being were overall modest and largely inconsistent. The only robust finding across subsets was a within-person association suggesting that days of higher than typical active social use were associated with lower positive affect. Notably, passive social use, which is among the strongest negative predictors of well-being in self-report studies, showed no reliable association under device logged measurement. Overall, these findings suggest that the psychological consequences of actual smartphone use behavior are more limited and more context-dependent than self-report studies imply, underscoring the importance of measurement methods in research on digital technology and well-being.

articles.title: Why Computational Cognitive Science? Specifying Social Science Theories as Cognitive Agents
articles.authors: Dohyun Ahn
articles.abstract: Social science theories about how people and environments change each other are mostly stated in words. Verbal statements leave open the quantities and functional forms needed to derive outcomes. Tests of association cannot distinguish the individual rules that could have produced an association, and causal structures established separately are rarely combined. Computational cognitive science offers a remedy: it specifies theories as rules that generate individual judgment and choice, runs the rules, and checks before data collection whether rival rules can be distinguished. Cognitive agent modeling adapts this practice to theories of person–environment relations. Four causal structures recur in social science: the environment changes people, people select their environments, the two change each other over time, and environmental effects differ across people. Cognitive agent modeling specifies these structures as four components of one agent: learning, choice, feedback, and individual differences. The article compares the approach with other computational approaches and works through media effects theories as a case, giving an example specification and four propositions. In a simulation, three rival explanations of crime viewing and fear yielded positive mean correlations, and a design alternating assigned and freely chosen exposure identified the generating specification in 96% to 100% of data sets.

articles.title: From Associations to Theories to an Atlas: Building a Cumulative Causal Science of Autism
articles.authors: Joshua Ewen
articles.abstract: Stakeholders are concerned that we have not made as much usable progress in autism research as we would want, given that approximately 100,000 papers have been published concerning the condition over the last 100 years. In this chapter, we identify that usable knowledge in the clinical, policy and support realms refers to causal knowledge. In the first half, we diagnose why this causal knowledge is particularly challenging to achieve within the constraints of psychological and cognitive-neuroscientific research, fields in which we typically have to rely on correlation rather than experimental manipulation. The gap between correlation (the information we have access to) and causation (the conclusions we need to make) is related to a large degree to addressing the likelihood of alternative causal paths that are able to explain the observed correlations, and falsifying these alternative causal paths is a primary key to closing the gap and arriving at causal conclusions. In the second half, we prescribe a falsification-centric approach toward approximating causality combined with a quantification of remaining paths. This aggregation will result in an atlas of evidence for and against causal claims in the condition. This approach focuses on empirical opportunities to empirically falsify “unnatural” constructs important to the various autism causal hypotheses as well as falsification of candidate causal relationships between those constructs. Moreover, we are able to accumulate prior results from the 100,000+ papers prior to planning additional data collection in a way that is independent of contemporaneous or even current assumptions in autism research and in a way that circumvents the working memory limitations of any particular researcher, clinician or advocate.

articles.title: Self-report and administrative adversity measures can have divergent associations with adult cognition: Evidence from 10 years of data
articles.authors: Nicole Walasek; Stefan Vermeent; Willem Frankenhuis
articles.abstract: Adversity research typically relies on self-report or aggregates of administrative data, rarely combining measures from both data sources over time. Here, we leverage Dutch administrative data and self-report measures to enable fine-grained, longitudinal tracking of individuals’ environments over a decade. We examine associations between five adversity dimensions—neighborhood threat, unpredictability in neighborhood threat, crime victimization, material deprivation, and health issues—with executive functioning and working memory in two adult samples (N = 1,024; N = 737). Self-report and administrative measures were only moderately correlated, suggesting they capture partially distinct adversity facets. We find that associations with cognitive outcomes mainly occur for neighborhood-level measures. Critically, although associations with administrative and self-report measures converged for some cognitive outcomes, they diverged for others. Specifically, self-reported adversity predicted intact or lowered performance, while administrative measures predicted intact or enhanced performance. These findings highlight the importance of illuminating the effects of adversity through multiple lenses.

articles.title: Navigating Digital Platforms in Adolescence: A Population‑Based Study of Online Sexual Experiences and Violations
articles.authors: Lia Ferschmann; Sjur Skjørshammer Sætren; Katrin Chauviré-Geib; Ann-Christin Haag; Miriam Rassenhofer; Olivia Dimitrijevic; Per Moum Hellevik; Else-Marie Augusti; Gertrud Sofie Hafstad
articles.abstract:
Background Digital platforms provide contexts for both normative adolescent sexual exploration and potential victimization. We lack understanding of the diversity of experiences adolescents encounter, and importantly, and how they subjectively appraise them. How a young person subjectively perceives an event may impact associations with health.
Methods This preregistered study used population-based self-report data from 3,675 adolescents aged 12–16 years to examine the prevalence of different online sexual experiences and violations, ranging from sharing sexual content to having nude images spread on social media. Additionally, the study probes several measures of subjective appraisals, including how distressing experiences were, regret and assessments of the extent to which one felt one was forced or tricked into the experience. Generalized linear models were used to examine associations between cumulative exposure to online sexual experiences and violations and mental health symptoms (Hopkins Symptom Checklist), somatic symptoms (Children’s Somatic Symptoms Inventory), and current and peak subjective distress related to these experiences. Regret was examined as a potential moderator. Logistic regression examined the history of offline sexual abuse by an adult as a risk factor.
Results By age 16, 49% of adolescents reported at least one online sexual experience or violation. Greater cumulative exposure was associated with more mental and somatic symptoms and higher current and peak subjective distress. Associations with symptoms remained even when accounting for symptoms from two years prior, family affluence, removing most severe items, and excluding participants reporting being coerced or tricked into the experience. Regret did not moderate exposure – subjective distress associations. Offline sexual abuse by an adult substantially increased the odds of having online sexual experiences or violations. Girls reported more coercion and subjective distress related to online sexual experiences, although boys were less likely to provide data on these measures.
Conclusions Digital contexts should be recognized as important developmental arenas in which adolescents navigate sexuality and intimacy, and where normative exploratory processes and potential risks co-occur. Future research should examine the socio-contextual factors that may render some online sexual experiences detrimental to health, informing efforts to create safer digital spaces that support adolescents’ exploration while protecting them from harm.

articles.title: Cheaper vegetarian meals reduce unhealthy add-on purchases without compensatory spending
articles.authors: Adéla Plechatá; Cecilie Fenja Strandsbjerg; Yanzhen Luo; Kristian Steensen Nielsen
articles.abstract: Price interventions are proposed to promote sustainable diets, yet real-world spillover effects are rarely tested. In three university canteens (94,740 transactions), one lowered vegetarian and increased meat buffet prices for 15 weeks. Unhealthy add-on purchases fell 1.09 percentage points relative to controls, a 26% relative reduction. Cheaper vegetarian lunches involved comparable portions and no more add-ons than meat lunches. We find no evidence that price differentiation shifts unhealthy consumption elsewhere.

articles.title: The Precision Trap: On the Idealization of Mathematics in Psychology
articles.authors: Sepehrdad Rahimian
articles.abstract: Calls for greater precision and mathematization in psychology are often motivated by the hope that they will help overcome the field's theoretical problems. While mathematics undoubtedly contributes to scientific progress, this paper questions the idea that an increase in mathematization, in itself, constitutes progress. First, it examines the tradeoffs of precision, arguing that making a theory more precise can change what is being studied, reduce its functionality, and sometimes lend an unwarranted authority to its claims. It also considers examples of non-mathematical yet successful psychological approaches. Second, the paper introduces the Mathematization Bind. Under a realist standard, mathematical precision cannot, by itself, establish that a theory has moved closer to Reality, as the history of the luminiferous aether illustrates. Under a pragmatic standard, the value of mathematics depends on what it enables us to accomplish, relative to the goals of inquiry. Neither perspective justifies treating greater mathematization as scientific progress by default. The paper also questions the tendency to regard an idealized image of physics as the model of scientific maturity. It concludes that the appropriate role and degree of mathematization in psychology should be determined by what it actually contributes to scientific inquiry, rather than by expectations about what a mature science ought to look like.

articles.title: Trail Making Tests in Extended Reality: A Critical Review with Implications for Cognitive Ageing
articles.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis
articles.abstract: Extended reality (XR) versions of the Trail Making Test and Color Trails Test are promising for assessing and training cognition in older adults. However, each XR adaptation is a new instrument, whose display, interaction technique, timing rules and layouts may change what it measures. This critical narrative review maps these implementations by software lineage and appraises their evidence for assessment and training against common criteria. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), whose source code was inspected, serves as a measurement case. XR trail-making tests showed convergence with paper and computerised versions, varying by test part and sample, and clinical group differences (e.g., Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment). However, gaps in reliability (e.g., randomised forms), validation (e.g., norms, prospective samples) and reporting (e.g., error handling, build identity) emerged, and no training benefit attributable to the trail-making component was identified. The TMT-VR case shows how interaction technique, timing rule, error handling and unlogged layouts shape a score's meaning. Future tests should log layouts and events, estimate alternate-form reliability and undergo prospective validation, and training trials should isolate the trail-making component. Several XR trail-making tests have moved beyond feasibility, and reported tolerability during supervised sessions supports further evaluation in older adults.

articles_hidden.title: Which Distortion gets confused? A Controlled Comparison of Language Models for Dominant Cognitive Distortion Classification
articles_hidden.authors: Rishi Gnanasekar; Caleb J. Siefert
articles_hidden.abstract:
Cognitive Distortions are unhelpful thinking
patterns that Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
(CBT) aims to identify and restructure, so
classifying cognitive distortions is a crucial
process for reframing. The classification
becomes difficult as the data is limited, and
the data are imbalanced most of the time. We
study dominant distortion classification on
the publicly available Therapist Q&A dataset
(Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021) where the anno-
tator agreement on the dominant distortion is
low (34%). Using the annotated distorted span
as input, we compare TF-IDF baselines with
RoBERTa, DeBERTa-v3 and MentalBERT
(with and without focal loss) over three seeds,
reporting accuracy, macro F1 and Cohen’s
kappa with significance tests. The encoders
reach 0.39 to 0.44 accuracy, well above the
majority-class baseline (0.15), the three cross-
entropy encoders are not significantly different
from each other, while the weighted focal loss
is worse. An error analysis shows that errors
concentrate on a small group of overlapping
distortions, mainly All-or-nothing thinking,
Magnification and Mental filter, which
suggests that unclear category boundaries limit
performance more than model choice.

articles_hidden.title: The Governed Heart:  Institutional Emotion Regulation through Policy, Proclamation, and Proxy
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas Paul Camp; Brett Quaid Ford
articles_hidden.abstract: Governments, schools, hospitals, companies, and myriad other organizations structure institutional life and mobilize large numbers of people to accomplish what they cannot do alone. Institutions also regulate something less visible, but equally consequential: the emotions of their constituents. We introduce institutional emotion regulation as the formal processes by which institutions, through organizations, seek to influence the emotions people have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions. Research across the social sciences has examined how particular organizations attempt to shape affective experiences, but these literatures have largely developed in disciplinary silos or domain-specific settings. We propose that these phenomena reflect a distinct level of emotion regulation, characterized by emotion goals held by organizations and pursued through formal institutional means. We develop a framework that crosses four established stages of emotion regulation – targeting situations, attention, appraisals, and responses – with three distinctive vectors of institutional influence: policies, the rules and structures that shape people’s environments; proclamations, communications directed toward the public; and proxies, the agents who act on behalf of the organization. Our framework provides a common language for understanding how institutions influence emotional life at scale and suggests novel directions for psychological study while surfacing broader questions for society around the appropriate use of this influence.

articles_hidden.title: Children adjust behavior in novel social environments to reflect local prosocial norms inferred from brief exposure
articles_hidden.authors: Kari Britt Schroeder; Laura Nelson; Peter Blake
articles_hidden.abstract: Stark cultural variation in prosocial behavior, as elicited with economic experiments, is evident despite the high mobility of humans. Conformity to local norms has been posited to play an integral role in the maintenance of this variation. Experiments suggest that adults indeed rapidly infer pro- and antisocial norms in new or altered social environments and adjust their behavior to reflect the inferred norms. Studies of the ontogeny of prosocial behavior show that by middle childhood, children’s prosocial behavior conforms to that of local adults. Furthermore, by this stage, children are susceptible to the manipulation of explicit normative information. However, their propensity to extract or infer normative information from the environment and change their behavior accordingly has not been investigated. Here, we assess whether children 1) rapidly infer local prosocial norms in a novel, realistic social environment, 2) extend these inferences to norms for unobserved behaviors, and 3) alter their behavior in the novel environment to align with the inferred norms while still 4) maintaining their baseline prosocial behavior outside of the novel environment. We used questionnaires to measure children’s perceived pro- and antisocial descriptive norms in their Own Neighborhoods as well as in a novel “Neighborhood X,” to which they were introduced via a slideshow. Norms for Neighborhood X diverged drastically dependent upon which slideshow they witnessed (Prosocial or Antisocial condition), a result robust to the exclusion of questions about norms for behaviors observed in the slideshow. Children’s perceptions of prosocial norms in their Own Neighborhoods predicted their prosocial behavior (Dictator Game) in their Own Neighborhood. Moreover, even though information about giving behavior was not presented in the slideshow, inferred norms for Neighborhood X predicted children’s prosocial behavior in that neighborhood as well. These changes in prosocial behavior were transitory and specific to Neighborhood X; prosocial behavior in a separate “Helping Task” was best predicted by prosocial norms within the children’s Own Neighborhoods. Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that humans have a propensity to rapidly infer and conform to local prosocial norms, thus maintaining group differences in prosocial behavior, and further indicate that this propensity is in operation by middle childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Multiple Methods for Visualizing Human Language: A Tutorial for Social and Behavioural Scientists
articles_hidden.authors: Veerle Celine Eijsbroek; August Nilsson; Leon Ackermann; Zhuojun Gu; Clara Wiebel; Adithya V Ganesan; Katarina Kjell; H. Andrew Schwartz; Oscar Nils Erik Kjell
articles_hidden.abstract:
Humans use language to communicate psychological experiences. Advancements in Natural Language
Processing have enabled researchers to quantitatively study and assess psychological states and
behaviors through language (e.g., well-being and mental health). Insights from language analyses are
often best conveyed through visualizations. Data-driven visualizations of how language statistically
relates to psychological dimensions can help interpret assessment scores, uncover meaningful patterns,
and understand the intricate relationships between language use and mental states. Visualizations can
be used to differentiate between related constructs (e.g., How does language related to depression versus
anxiety differ?), understand the validity of assessment tools (e.g., Does the language related to high
depression severity match with depression theory?), and explain language-based assessments (e.g.,
Which language is indicative of higher depression severity in a language-based assessment?).

This tutorial demonstrates how to transform language data into visual insights using the text and topics
packages in R. We provide practical guidance on creating four types of visualizations based on different
language analysis techniques, examining how language use patterns are statistically associated with a
psychological construct. We visualize 1) individual words and phrases (n-grams), 2) topics (word
clusters), 3) words in the word embedding space, and 4) relevant language examples. These different
visualizations offer complementary perspectives, visualizing linguistic elements from individual words
to overarching topics and text examples. The underlying methods range from correlations between
individual words to more advanced techniques, including topic modeling and Large Language Models.
By making these methods accessible, this tutorial aims to empower researchers to use language
visualizations for meaningful, data-driven insights.

articles_hidden.title: A Placebo Cannot Be Psychedelic: Why psychedelic trials need dose, not mimicry, as their control
articles_hidden.authors: Wolfgang Liedtke
articles_hidden.abstract: In a recently published Viewpoint, Yang-et-al propose masking high-dose psilocybin trials with a multidrug comparator engineered to reproduce the psychedelic experience. Their objective, restoration of the gold-standard of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled standard, is well-intentioned, but the proposed approach dissolves the concept it aims to rescue. A placebo permits to understand the impact of expectation because it is inert. Recent neural circuit-level results in mice shows how concretely expectation affects behavior, relying on in-vivo experimentation that separates placebo effect from active treatment. A comparator that recreates the psychedelic experience must engage the circuits that generate it, becoming a second active treatment whose own pharmacology confounds any eventual difference placebo-active, possibly in both directions. Some interventions, from topical TRP-channel activators (capsaicin, menthol) to classic psychedelics, cannot be matched by an inert control. Dose-controlled designs represent the remaining option where well-intentioned mimicry fails: their main possible bias might work against the drug. Dose-controlled designs can be paired with external controls and approval tied to mandatory postmarketing evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Comparing Logit and Probit Coefficients From Same-Sample Nested Models: Adapting the (Revised) KHB Method to an SEM Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Wolfgang Wagner; Benjamin Nagengast
articles_hidden.abstract: Karlson et al. (2012) suggested an estimation strategy for logistic and probit regression models, the so-called KHB method, which allows differences between regression coefficients in same-sample nested regression models to be interpreted. We introduce the pseudo mediation model (PMM), which implements the KHB method in a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework. The PMM has several advantages over the “standard” KHB method: First, missing data can be handled under less restrictive assumptions. Second, predictors can be included as latent variables to avoid bias due to measurement error. Finally, nested data structures and survey weights can be accounted for. We illustrate the method with empirical examples.

articles_hidden.title: A systematic review of recruitment and retention within randomised controlled trials of adults with Down Syndrome
articles_hidden.authors: Aimee Wilkinson; Jade Eloise Norris; Nicola Mills; Victoria Nimmo-Smith; Angela Hassiotis; Dheeraj Rai; Alba X Realpe
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Adults with Down Syndrome (DS) face significant health inequalities. Evidence from high-quality randomised controlled trials (RCTs) for interventions are lacking, and there is a perceived difficulty regarding recruiting and retaining participants with DS. 
Aims: This systematic review aimed to examine planned vs. actual recruitment and retention rates of RCTs involving adults with DS, summarising reported facilitators of and barriers to participation.
Method: MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and EMBASE databases were searched systematically to retrieve RCTs of any intervention involving adults with DS =>16yrs, published to 07/12/2023, with a second search in April 2025. Searches were also conducted on trial registries, and reference lists reviewed. Trial design, planned and achieved sample size, retention rate, and recruitment and retention strategies were extracted 26/02/2024-18/03/2024 for the first search, and in August 2025 for the updated search (Prospero: CRD42023447126; registered: 04/09/2023). 
Results: After deduplication, 1,622 articles underwent title and abstract screening, with 89 full texts reviewed. Five additional papers were identified from reference lists. 1,785 adults with DS were randomised to 44 included RCTs. Most studies did not pre-register their protocol nor target sample size (n=16 reported target N; 36.36%) and typically recruited small samples: 13 recruited N ≥40 (29.55%; N range=8-337, median N=25, IQR 21.75). Attrition by primary outcome also varied widely (0-47%).
Conclusions: There is a paucity of high-quality, large-scale RCTs involving adults with DS, and challenges related to participation rates (e.g., stringent exclusion criteria, consent challenges, and study burden). Strategies to overcome challenges in recruitment and retention to such trials are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: How do time of day and location influence affect experience? A passive sensing study
articles_hidden.authors: Simon M. Li; Molly Patapoff; Aanika Schueler; Qimin Liu; David E. Gard; Carlos Busso; Jukka-Pekka Onnela; Daniel Fulford
articles_hidden.abstract: Momentary emotional experience is shaped by the contexts in which individuals are embedded, yet little is known about how time spent in certain locations (e.g., at home versus in public spaces) relates to affect in daily life. In the current study, 74 young adults completed 14 days of smartphone-based ecological momentary assessment and GPS-based geolocation. We examined three contextual dimensions in relation to momentary affect (happiness, anxiety, and sadness) in young adults: environmental context (at home versus outside), recent exposure duration (time spent at home in the preceding three hours), and temporal context (time of day and day of week). Multilevel models indicated that participants reported higher happiness and lower anxiety in the evening relative to morning, and higher happiness on weekends than on weekdays. Within individuals, being at home (and time spent at home) was associated with lower happiness than being outside the home. Furthermore, the exploratory analysis suggested that the association between time spent at home and lower happiness was stronger among individuals who typically spent less time at home. These findings suggest that temporal and environmental contexts are associated with momentary happiness, whereas environmental context was not associated with anxiety or sadness.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual distinctiveness underlies apparent emotion-specific advantages in facial expression detection
articles_hidden.authors: Erika Bucci; Giacomo Handjaras; Giada Lettieri; Luca Cecchetti
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans are assumed to prioritize facial expressions because of the evolutionary significance of their affective content. Here, we show that this assumption does not survive rigorous control of perceptual structure. Across three studies integrating preregistered visual search experiments, geometric modeling of facial expressions, and eye-tracking data, we tested whether detection advantages for happy and angry faces reflect low-level visual salience rather than emotion. To this end, we combined frequentist interval testing with a predefined smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) and Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses. Behavioral and oculomotor measures reliably predicted emotion category when expressions were presented at full, perceptually unbalanced intensity. By contrast, when expression intensity was matched, both interval testing and Bayesian ROPE analyses supported the absence of a practically meaningful effect. In addition, detection speed and accuracy were best explained by geometric deviation from a neutral face, independent of emotional category. These findings indicate that apparent emotion advantages in visual search arise from perceptual salience rather than privileged access to emotion, challenging evolutionary accounts of attentional prioritization.

articles_hidden.title: Child Multilingualisms Beyond WEIRD Contexts: Evidence from Asia and Africa
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra Paquette; Leher Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Who is the language learner represented in language acquisition research? Despite the prevalence and diversity of multilingual childhoods, theories of early language development remain grounded in monolinguals from Euro-American contexts, while multilingual research has concentrated on limited populations/settings. This review examines multilingual language development during the first three years across Asia and Africa, attending to diversity within and between regions. Research on input, speech perception, word recognition, and vocabulary indicate that multilingual infants flexibly adapt to linguistic ecologies, but vary in developmental pathways. We argue that multilingualism should be conceptualized not as a categorical characteristic, but as a multidimensional ecology structured by language combinations, caregiving arrangements, social functions, socioeconomic conditions, and colonial histories. We conclude with a research agenda that broadens empirical and linguistic coverage, improves measurement of multilingual experiences, and centers community-informed priorities. A globally adequate science of language development requires building theory from children’s diverse multilingual realities.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating the Parental Burnout Assessment in parents of children with and without complex care needs: Measurement invariance, group differences, and the correlates of sociodemographic characteristics
articles_hidden.authors: Nathalie Patty; Caro Henrica Catharina Lemmen; Carlo Schuengel; Karen van Meeteren; Marjolijn Ketelaar; Maartje Luijk; Agnes M. Willemen
articles_hidden.abstract: The study aim was to evaluate the measurement invariance of the Parental Burnout Assessment (PBA), across parents of children with complex care needs (CCN) and parents of children without CCN, compare burnout scores between these groups, and explore how sociodemographic characteristics relate to parental burnout within each parenting context. The PBA was completed by 337 parents of children with CCN and 329 parents who did not have a child with CCN. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the theoretically proposed four-factor structure of the PBA, encompassing exhaustion in the parental role, feelings of being fed up, contrast with pervious parental self, and emotional distancing. A subsequent second-order CFA indicated that these four dimensions could be explained by a single overarching factor, parental burnout. Multigroup CFA supported scalar invariance across groups for both the four-factor model and the second-order model, indicating that the observed group differences in PBA scores reflect true differences rather than measurement bias. Parents of children with CCN reported significantly higher PBA scores than parents of children without CCN (d = 1.33, p < .001). Among the sociodemographic characteristics examined, we found that being a mother of a child with CCN was associated with substantially higher PBA scores compared to being a father of a child with CCN. This gender difference was smaller among parents of children without CCN. Parental age, ethnicity, educational attainment, being single parent, the number of children, and minimum and maximum age of the child were not associated with higher parental burnout scores. Findings underscore the heightened vulnerability for parental burnout among parents of children with CCN compared to parents of children without CCN while also providing further evidence for the suitability of the PBA as a research instrument for assessing parental burnout across the caregiving context of being a parent of a child with CCN or not.

articles_hidden.title: Facilitation by Irrelevant Distractors Under High Perceptual Load: Suppression or Controlled Distractor Prioritization?
articles_hidden.authors: Greta Manini; Francisco Garre-Frutos; Fabiano Botta; Elisa Martín-Arévalo; Juan Lupiáñez
articles_hidden.abstract: Perceptual load theory is a key framework in visual attention research, demonstrating that under high-load conditions, fully irrelevant distractors are no longer processed and do not disrupt task performance. In our recent work (Manini et al., 2026), we replicated this effect. However, we also found that under high load, the distractor not only failed to impair performance but actually led to faster reaction times (RTs) in distractor-present trials. In the attentional capture literature, this reversed effect is typically considered to reflect distractor suppression. However, in the perceptual load task, where the distractor is placed outside the relevant search array, suppression should not logically lead to faster responses. Furthermore, the faster responses were accompanied by increased error rates, leading us to hypothesize that this reversed effect may reflect some form of distractor prioritization rather than distractor suppression. To test this hypothesis, we first analyzed the consistency of this effect across all available open-data resources using the Forster and Lavie (2008b) task. We then reanalyzed the same data, incorporating the spatial proximity between target and distractor as an additional variable: distractors appearing near the target strongly drove the reversed RT effect, while distractors presented far from the target led to increased error rates. These findings challenge the idea that high perceptual load prevents the processing of irrelevant stimuli. Moreover, they suggest that faster RTs in distractor-present conditions do not necessarily indicate distractor suppression, as commonly assumed in attentional capture research, offering new insight into the interpretation of behavioral observations in this field.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping Leadership in Teams: An Empirically Grounded Taxonomy of Formal and Peer Leadership Roles.
articles_hidden.authors: Charlotte Marie Edelmann; Filip Boen; Jeroen Stouten; Katrien Fransen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Formal and peer (informal) leaders play crucial roles in fostering team effectiveness and member well-being. Although leadership research has examined a wide range of leader behaviors, it remains fragmented and typically focuses on either formal or peer leaders rather than both. Moreover, no empirically grounded taxonomy captures the breadth of leadership behaviors across hierarchical levels.

Design/methodology/approach: To address this gap, we developed an inductively derived, literature-integrated taxonomy of leadership functions. We first conducted qualitative interviews with 35 employees varying in hierarchical level, education, sector, and gender. Qualitative content analysis identified leadership functions enacted by formal and peer leaders. Participants then completed individual and group card-sorting exercises to cluster these functions into higher-order leadership roles.

Findings: The taxonomy comprised 10 formal and 10 peer leadership roles. Comparison with existing leadership frameworks showed where prior research converges with and extends the leadership functions identified by participants.

Originality: This integrative taxonomy provides a practice-informed framework for advancing leadership theory and informing leadership development across organizational contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Testing Socio-Perceptual Equigenesis with Biophilic Interventions: A Virtual Reality Eye-Tracking Study Across Neighborhood Socioeconomic Status
articles_hidden.authors: Paula Latorre; Cleiton Pons Ferreira; Aurora Molina-Muñoz; Sergio Castaño-Castaño; Miguel Morales Navas; Francisco Nieto-Escamez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Inequity in access to urban green spaces perpetuates marked disparities in psychological well-being in cities. The present study evaluates whether micro-scale biophilic interventions in virtual environments act as a socio-perceptual equalizer (Environmental Equigenesis Hypothesis) and modulate attention through oculomotor patterns of soft fascination (Attention Restoration Theory). Within this framework, 60 Hz eye-tracking integrated into Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) was used to capture implicit attentional dynamics objectively. Framed within a mixed methods project registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) after data collection and before any inferential analysis, and given the density of the data obtained, this manuscript reports exclusively the quantitative block focused on oculomotor and psychometric triangulation, reserving the qualitative analysis for a subsequent report. A sample of 75 participants exposed to 360° virtual tours evaluated low-, medium-, and high-socioeconomic-status (SES) neighborhoods under Original and Enhanced conditions. Eye-tracking revealed that the biophilic design did not alter the total volume of fixations but significantly reduced the average fixation duration, a pattern compatible with the attentional coupling of soft fascination. In parallel, subjective increases in positive affect, liking, esthetic evaluation, and relaxation were observed, while perceived stress did not change significantly overall. No significant differences in esthetic evaluation between neighborhoods remained after the intervention, and the areas-of-interest (AOIs) metrics showed a different allocation of gaze across neighborhoods, partly because the interventions applied were not the same in each one. Eye-tracking complemented the self-report data, although the main equigenesis findings rest on the psychometric measures.
Keywords: virtual reality, eye-tracking, biophilic design, attention restoration theory, environmental equigenesis, socioeconomic status

articles_hidden.title: Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater! Why "preregistration" is still a useful term: Commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)
articles_hidden.authors: Priya Silverstein; Lisa Spitzer; Lukas Wallrich; Josefina Weinerova
articles_hidden.abstract: This is a commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025), published in Avances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science (AMPPS). As per AMPPS submission guidelines, no abstract is included for commentaries.

articles_hidden.title: How Self-Location Predicts the Degree and Quality of the Felt Sense of Connection
articles_hidden.authors: MARIE SESTER; Glenn Hartelius; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has typically examined how self-location in the head or heart is associated with traits and behavior, yet its link to relationality—specifically the felt sense of connection—remains underexplored. This study investigated how dispositional self-location predicts the embodied experience of being relationally linked to others and the world. We initially developed the Dispositional Self-Location Questionnaire (DSLQ), an association-based instrument designed to minimize potential subjective bias in participant reporting of self-location. Using this measure, we categorized a U.S. sample of 218 adults who had reported a strong experience of connection as head-locators or heart-locators and assessed them on self-construal, self-expansiveness, connectedness, and perceived qualities of connection. Head-locators reported firmer self-boundaries, emphasizing independence, rationality, and decision-making. In contrast, Heart-locators scored significantly higher on connectedness to both self and world, and on metapersonal self-construal, describing their connections as close, warm, caring, and authentic. These findings suggest that self-location functions as a somatic attentional stance that anticipates the experiential boundary between self and other: the head favors separation and autonomy, while the heart favors openness and expanded belonging.
