articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Polyphasia and Cognitive Dissonance: An Integrative Model for Understanding Inconsistency Management Within Social Representations Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Thiago Mikael Silva; Adriano Roberto Afonso do Nascimento
articles_hidden.abstract:
The aim of this study was to explore the interrelationship between cognitive
polyphasia and cognitive dissonance in the management of contradictions. We argue
that both concepts maintain a circular relationship. To support this position, we
establish a theoretical path structured around four core axes: 1) the recognition that
Festinger and his followers already considered dissonance management mechanisms
that, much like cognitive polyphasia, maintain inconsistency; 2) from a diachronic
perspective, dissonance can stem from cognitive polyphasia; 3) from a synchronic
perspective, the varieties of cognitive polyphasia can be systematized within the
functional approach to cognitive dissonance; 4) this systematization raises questions
regarding the self and identity, bringing Social Representations Theory closer to
contemporary models of the self. Throughout this path, we outline an integrative
model for the study of inconsistency management, offering brief considerations on the
challenges that future research must overcome.

articles_hidden.title: It’s about time: Specifying time zero for target trial emulation in psychological research
articles_hidden.authors: Dongning Ren; Wen Wei Loh
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists often rely on observational studies for causal evidence, which raises the question of how to strengthen the design of observational studies for causal inference. One widely used approach in medical research is target trial emulation (TTE). In this tutorial, we introduce TTE to psychological research, with particular emphasis on its cornerstone concept that is routinely ignored in practice: time zero. Following a brief primer on TTE, we foreground time zero and highlight its critical role in improving valid causal inferences from observational data. Using examples drawn from psychological research, we systematically enumerate all possible permutations of the time zero components to show how their misalignment can introduce systematic biases, including selection bias, post-treatment confounding, treatment-dependent (in)eligibility, and immortal time bias, even when all baseline confounders are measured. To address this, we develop a decision framework for integrating time zero into research practices and offer practical recommendations. Through a running example of workplace AI use and employee burnout, we demonstrate how clearly specifying time zero clarifies causal questions, prevents many design-based biases, and strengthens internal validity. We further emphasize that time zero alignment is only one design feature of a strong observational study, and we delineate the boundaries of TTE, cautioning against the misconception that it is a magic fix that automatically delivers causal conclusions. We conclude that explicitly justifying time zero is a necessary step toward improving the rigor and transparency of causal research in psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Mediterranean-style dietary components and self-reported depression: a cross-sectional analysis of 502,359 UK adults in the UK Biobank cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Haidi Martinidou; Donald M Lyall
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mediterranean-style diet adherence has been associated with lower depression prevalence, but studies are typically small and adjust for few confounders. We aimed to estimate cross-sectional associations between individual Mediterranean-style dietary components and reported depression, and how far they attenuate with broader sociodemographic and lifestyle adjustment.
Methods: Cross-sectional analysis of the UK Biobank cohort (N=502,359). Six self-reported dietary variables - oily fish, non-oily fish, fresh fruit, salad and raw vegetables, cooked vegetables and processed meat - were tested against self-reported depression using binary logistic regression, modelled individually with progressive adjustment (full adjustment: age, sex, smoking, medication, Townsend deprivation index, month of assessment, educational attainment), then all together in one multivariable model.
Results: 28,194 participants (5.6%) reported depression. Fully adjusted, higher intakes of oily fish (odds ratio[OR]=0.900, 95% CI [confidence intervals] 0.888 to 0.912), non-oily fish (OR=0.931, 0.917 to 0.945), fresh fruit (OR=0.974, 0.966 to 0.982), salad and raw vegetables (OR=0.970, 0.964 to 0.976) and cooked vegetables (OR=0.967, 0.960 to 0.974) were each associated with lower odds. 
Conclusion: Individual components of a Mediterranean-style diet showed small, consistent associations with lower odds of self-reported depression, not explained by the measured confounders. The design does not support causal interpretation. For researchers, prospective designs with repeated dietary measurement and diagnosed outcomes are needed; for practitioners and policymakers, these estimates do not support dietary components as a substitute for established treatment or as a stand-alone prevention target.

articles_hidden.title: Looping effects and the cognitive source of epistemic injustices: A simulation study
articles_hidden.authors: Axel Constant; Christophe Gauld; Ana Gomez-Carrillo; Laurence Kirmayer; Karl Friston
articles_hidden.abstract: Patient–clinician interactions are central to diagnosis and treatment in mental health care. They involve inferential processes grounded in patients’ reports of symptoms and clinicians’ interpretations of signs. These processes are liable to microdynamic looping effects that drive diagnostic belief formation. In facing the hermeneutic challenge of reaching a shared ascription of the patient’s condition, such looping effects can lead to misalignment and give rise to epistemic injustice if a credibility deficit exists between the patient and the clinician. In this paper, we use the active inference framework to develop a computational model of looping microdynamics that captures how patients and clinicians reciprocally interpret symptoms, attribute causes, and negotiate diagnostic categories over time. We present a simulation study showing how specific interactional patterns can amplify or mitigate credibility deficits, depending in part on clinicians’ attributional attitudes toward patients’ self-interpretations. Our results suggest that, in contexts of diagnostic disagreement, positive disconfirmation—offering an alternative explanatory framing rather than simply negating the patient’s perspective—may reduce the risk of epistemic injustice. Overall, the model highlights how looping microdynamics structure mutual belief formation in clinical encounters and how attention to these dynamics can support more epistemically responsible clinical communication.

articles_hidden.title: Data Transparency in Industrial, Work, and Organizational Psychology: A Primer on Data Sharing and Documentation of Data Reuse
articles_hidden.authors: Maie Stein; Richard Janzen; Cort W. Rudolph; Hannes Zacher
articles_hidden.abstract: Data transparency is fundamental for evaluating the validity of empirical findings, supporting cumulative knowledge building, and strengthening the credibility of science in society. However, data sharing (i.e., making research data available to others) and transparent documentation of data reuse (i.e., reporting the use of the same data across multiple publications) are not yet standard practice in industrial, work, and organizational (IWO) psychology. The aim of this primer is to discuss the important role of these data transparency practices in advancing open science and to provide practical guidance for the adoption of these practices in IWO psychology. We review the benefits and challenges of data sharing and outline recommendations for researchers, reviewers, and journal editors in IWO psychology to support its implementation. We also examine the implications of data reuse for the interpretation and accumulation of empirical evidence and propose several approaches for transparently documenting data reuse.

articles_hidden.title: Moral Preferences for Avoiding Non-Lethal Human Injury over Property Damage in Autonomous Vehicle Accidents
articles_hidden.authors: Kiichi INARIMORI; Yuri Tanaka; Takashi Hikasa; Tsutomu Sawai
articles_hidden.abstract: Given the rapid development of autonomous vehicle (AV) technologies, recent studies, such as the Moral Machine Experiment, have examined people’s moral judgments in trolley-style dilemmas, where AVs must choose between unavoidable outcomes, often involving whether to change course to save a greater number of lives. However, fatal injuries represent only a subset of harms caused by traffic agents; most traffic accidents are non-fatal or involve only property damage. The present study focuses on trade-offs between human harm and property damage, examining whether the principle of the priority of human over property (PPHP)—reflected in some ethical and legal guidelines—is consistently supported by the public. Across a series of online experiments, we investigated whether people’s path preferences in scenarios where an AV must choose between avoiding human harm and avoiding property damage align with PPHP. We manipulated several factors, including the severity of harm to the pedestrian, the value of the property, the observer’s perspective (first-person vs. third-person), the gender of the potential victim, and whether the passenger would bear legal liability. The results indicate that participants are more likely to prioritize avoiding property damage when the expected harm to humans is relatively low compared to the value of the property. This tendency is amplified when passengers are held legally liable and among participants with more utilitarian moral attitudes. These findings suggest that AV behavior strictly guided by PPHP is not always supported by lay moral judgments.

articles_hidden.title: Number personification and imaginary companions: Concurrent rather than developmental links in school-age children
articles_hidden.authors: Eiko Matsuda; Acer Yu-Chan Chang; Yusuke Moriguchi; Osamu Sakura
articles_hidden.abstract: Number personification (NP), the attribution of gender, age, or character to digits, is common among 9- to 12-year-olds, but its relationship to other forms of childhood personification remains unknown. Because NP and imaginary companions (ICs) share the attribution of personhood to non-living entities and high idiosyncrasy, we hypothesized that NP is a developmental extension of ICs. In a web survey, 2,193 Japanese mothers of children in grades 1--6 reported their child's current and past IC and NP status and fantasy orientation. Current ICs were reported for 15.1¥% of children, and current NP for 1.2¥%. Contrary to our hypothesis, past IC did not predict current NP; instead, children with a current IC had four times the odds of NP (odds ratio = 4.16). Grade, gender, and fantasy orientation were related to ICs but not, or only weakly, to NP. NP appears to co-occur with ICs rather than to follow them developmentally.

articles_hidden.title: Are Workplace Tolerance and Individual Autonomy associated with Work Engagement? —Mediation analyses with Psychological Safety and Intrinsic Motivation
articles_hidden.authors: Takazumi Ono; Ryota Shin; Aoba Tamura; Yukihiko Okada; Hiroko Costantini; Misato Nihei
articles_hidden.abstract: There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees. Although the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments. We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation. We used data from 1084 Japanese workers collected across four waves of online surveys and conducted causal mediation analyses. As a result, the presence of tolerant coworkers was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety (total effect = 0.296; proportion mediated = 29.7 %), whereas the absence of intolerant coworkers was not clearly associated with work engagement. Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation (total effect = 0.444), although the proportion mediated was modest (14.5 %). These findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD–R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.

articles_hidden.title: A Computational Approach to Search in Visual Working Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Aditi Singh; Andra Mihali; Wen-Chuang Chou; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Search in visual working memory (VWM) is  an important  process in everyday life, but it has so far not been investigated sufficiently using psychophysical and computational approaches. Here, we examine whether computational process models from the study of VWM and of visual search also apply to search in VWM. Participants performed a two-alternative VWM-based color localization task in which set size and color similarity were varied. We tested models with a resource-limited encoding stage and a Bayesian decision stage. We found that a variable-precision model fit the data well and that adding an item limit did not improve the fit. Next, we took a resource-rational approach, in which mean precision at each set size is set by optimizing a combination between behavioral performance and encoding cost. We found that a resource-rational model with an ad-hoc cost function captures behavior well, but not better than the best non-resource-rational model. Our results, albeit unsurprising, contribute to the evidence that search in VWM is very similar to search in perception.

articles_hidden.title: Benchmarking an automated speech recognition pipeline for Spanish-English bilingual preschoolers: Quantifying language input and output in daylong recordings.
articles_hidden.authors: Gaurab Subedi; Marvin Lavechin; Jorge Fonseca; Sarah Surrain
articles_hidden.abstract: Measuring how much of each language bilingual children hear and use in their daily lives requires transcribing long, naturalistic recordings, which is too costly to do by hand at scale. We benchmarked four WhisperX-based automatic speech recognition pipelines, differing in how speech is located and attributed to speakers, against expert transcripts of 168 five-minute clips (14 hours) drawn from daylong home recordings of 14 Spanish--English bilingual preschoolers. Word error rates across pipelines were high (69.5% to 82.0% overall), compared with 35.4% (key child) and 53.9% (adults) between expert coders. Running a child-centered voice type classifier (VTC2) before transcription attributed words to speakers far better than labeling speakers afterwards; we retained this pipeline (WER = 71.4%). Despite word-level errors, it preserved the rank order of clips; automated and manual counts of total and distinct words correlated at r = .83 to .93 for adults and the key child in each language. Agreement rose further at the recording level. Lexical diversity was recovered best: slopes for distinct words (0.79 to 0.88) were closer to one than for total words (0.53 to 0.77). The proportion of Spanish was underestimated (adults: 77% vs. 89%; key child: 70% vs. 90%), largely because WhisperX output short English phrases on brief, unclear audio. Open, inspectable pipelines can yield language-specific measures of bilingual adult input and child output, but precise word counts and language proportions require correction before direct interpretation. These estimates, from one Spanish--English community, will need re-estimating in other populations.

articles_hidden.title: Decisions About Expressing Subjective States Generalise Across Psychological Domain
articles_hidden.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles_hidden.abstract:
People routinely make decisions about how to express their internal psychological states to the
outside world. These communication choices can systematically influence the meaning observers
extract about the internal states of others. In psychological science, this is frequently observed in
the way people respond to self-report surveys. Quantitative cognitive models of these
communication choices, such as the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, translate
continuous psychological states into Likert-type responses. In doing so, the model can separate
internal experiences (latent states) from preferences for (or against) certain response options in
self-report scenarios. A key assumption of the LASARS model is that response style reflects a
stable individual characteristic that generalises across contexts. The present study tested this
assumption by examining whether response styles remain consistent across theoretically distinct
psychological domains. A sample of 145 adults completed four survey instruments assessing
sensation seeking, thinking styles, dark personality traits, and perceived control. We compared a
model in which response style parameters were estimated separately for each instrument with a
more parsimonious model in which response style was assumed to be identical across all
instruments. Response style parameters exhibited strong cross-instrument correlations, exceeding
the magnitude of correlations observed among latent states. Furthermore, constraining response
style to be shared across instruments produced virtually identical predictions of observed scores
and latent state estimates while reducing model complexity substantially. These findings provide
strong evidence that response style is a stable, domain-general characteristic. They also support
the conclusion that people use similar decision strategies to express their internal psychological
states across the different constructs they may wish or be asked to communicate.

articles_hidden.title: Linguistic Markers of Self-Representation Reflect Daily Emotional Experiences in an Expressive Writing Study
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Huang; Claire Whiting; Steven Mesquiti; Sofia S. Baran; Erik C Nook
articles_hidden.abstract: The words people use provide important insights into their emotional experiences. Several measures for tracking emotions through language have been developed, including sentiment (i.e., the positivity and negativity of language) and I-usage (first-person singular pronoun use, thought to reflect negative self-focus). However, emerging research using large language model embedding techniques has quantified not just if people use “I” but how they use it, yielding a measure of self-representation (i.e., how strongly people see themselves as “good” and “able” rather than “bad” and “unable”). This measure tracks mental health outcomes in psychotherapy. Given that emotions and emotion regulation are intimately connected to how we view ourselves, linguistic self-representations may also offer a means for assessing emotional experiences. Here, we examined the associations between participants’ linguistic self-representations and daily emotional experiences in a 14-day expressive writing study (N = 53). Within-person associations showed that on days when participants’ self-representation embedding scores were closer to “good” or “able,” they reported more positive and less negative emotions. At the between-person level, people with self-representations overall closer to “good” experienced lower negative emotional reactivity to expressive writing. These findings suggest that linguistic markers of self-representation hold promise as a tool for assessing emotional experiences, extending prior work linking it to mental health. Translations of these findings could contribute to earlier identification of changes in emotional functioning and provide new ways of assessing metrics of mental health through everyday language.

articles_hidden.title: Innateness is (still) an orienting principle for language development
articles_hidden.authors: Leher Singh; Marisa Casillas; Shanley E. M. Allen; Michael C. Frank; Caroline F Rowland
articles_hidden.abstract:
How humans come to acquire language has been a persistent object of philosophical and scientific inquiry, in part because it bears on fundamental questions about the nature of human cognition.
Classically, this field of inquiry has centered innateness as a critical component of language acquisition, traditionally characterizing innate capability in terms of richly specified, biologically endowed linguistic structure, such as Universal Grammar. Contemporary theories have evolved considerably from these earlier formulations and now present several differing candidates for innateness in language. Throughout this evolution, though, questions of innateness have remained central to theories of language acquisition, even as the nature of those questions has shifted in response to new sources of evidence. In this Perspective, we consider evidence from three complementary sources of evidence—linguistic diversity, human social interaction, and language models (LMs)—that together inform the question of what children must bring to the task of language learning. We conclude by identifying desiderata for theories of language acquisition that seek to specify the nature, scope, and explanatory role of innate contributions to language development.

articles_hidden.title: A mind-body disconnection? Discordance between thoughts about stress and cardiovascular stress responses
articles_hidden.authors: Audrey Merwin; Brett J. Peters; Elizabeth Haudrich; Abriana M Gresham; Ashley Tudder; Nathan Stuart; Jessica Lang; Kylee Bernel; Parastesh Sattari; Peggy Zoccola
articles_hidden.abstract: Stress responses are defined by mind-body interactions that engage both psychological and physiological processes. We provide foundational research investigating the mind-body connection during stress to ask: how do individuals’ thoughts about stressors align with their cardiovascular responses? 925 dyads (N = 1,850) anticipated, engaged in, and recovered from stress-inducing social-evaluative tasks. Analyses revealed that individuals’ self-reported and cardiovascular indices of stress were not significantly associated at any timepoint, bolstered by post-hoc Inclusion Bayes Factors supporting the null (vs. alternative) hypothesis. Meta-analytic results suggested the association between measures is effectively zero, indicating findings may generalize beyond a social interaction context and our primarily White, female, college-aged sample. These findings suggest individuals’ perceptions of stress may be distinct from their physiological stress responses, carry significant implications for the way we conceptualize and measure stress, and indicate that multi-method, full-body approaches are critical for a holistic understanding of the human stress response.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting the Radius of Trust Problem: Who Counts as “Most People”?
articles_hidden.authors: Anu Realo; Jüri Allik
articles_hidden.abstract: General trust in social surveys is usually measured with a Single-Item General Trust (SIGT) question that asks whether “most people” can be trusted. The concept of the radius of trust challenges this approach by highlighting that trust may vary with the social distance between those who express trust and those who are trusted. This has led to the addition of six specific trust questions to the World Values Survey (WVS) questionnaire since Wave 5, which ask respondents to rate their trust in their family, neighborhood, and people they know personally, as well as in people of another religion, people of another nationality, and people they meet for the first time. Analyzing respondents’ answers to the SIGT and six specific trust items in the Integrated Values Surveys (IVS) dataset (1981-2022) across 88 countries and territories and the three most recent survey waves, we find that trust is a complex construct whose invariant property across cultures is a fixed-length vector composed of the squares of its two components: ingroup and outgroup trust. The phrase “most people” in the SIGT question appears to refer to “familiar strangers”—people whom respondents do not know personally but are likely to encounter in everyday life. It is trust in these familiar strangers, rather than in more distant outgroups, which is most strongly associated with the Human Development Index. This association, however, becomes pronounced only at very high levels of human development.

articles_hidden.title: Distinct sensorimotor representations during combined action observation and motor imagery
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Scott; David Wright; Nicola Jane Hodges; Justine Magnuson; Sarah N Kraeutner
articles_hidden.abstract: The human sensorimotor system can represent actions in the absence of movement, termed motor simulation. These motor simulations can be perceptually (externally) driven through observation of an actor or cognitively (internally) driven through imagining movement. Although there is evidence humans can represent multiple actions simultaneously, whether different motor simulations can concurrently be represented is unclear. We investigated the capacity of the sensorimotor system to simultaneously represent observed (action observation; AO) and imagined actions (motor imagery; MI). Two competing hypotheses were tested concerning whether AO and MI could co-exist or not, The Dual Action Simulation Hypothesis (DASH) and Visual Guidance Hypothesis (VGH), respectively. Fifteen participants completed a functional magnetic resonance imagining (fMRI) study, requiring them to complete four distinct conditions involving imagination or observation of a rhythmical hand tapping action. Conditions involved: AO, AO with a counting task (i.e., with cognitive load), MI, or simultaneous AO and MI of different actions (AOMI). Through representational similarity analysis, AO and MI motor simulations were evidenced in the right ventral premotor cortex, supporting DASH over VGH. Multidimensional scaling of representational similarity data indicated a unique representational pattern for AOMI, differing from AO and MI across different dimensions. Whole-brain analyses were conducted, showing descriptive support for greater engagement of sensorimotor regions during AOMI vs. the summation of independent AO and MI conditions occurred, complementing findings from our representational similarity analysis. While dual motor simulations appear possible, our data suggests that the representational pattern of AOMI is distinct, producing super-additive sensorimotor activity. Neither DASH nor VGH adequately explain these data.

articles_hidden.title: Disasters and Sports in Dreams: Unexpected Selectivity in Dream Incorporation
articles_hidden.authors: Marcin Florkowski
articles_hidden.abstract:
Population-level indicators of interest in dream-related topics were analyzed using Google Trends for California, Texas, the Philippines, and the United Kingdom—areas with a combined population of more than 250 million—as well as at the global level. Media-salient natural disasters are reflected in dreams. The relative representation of sports-related and disaster-related content was compared between ordinary searches and dream-related searches.
Although sports overwhelmingly dominated waking interest, disaster-related content was represented about 24 times as strongly in dream-related searches as expected based on its relative share of ordinary searches. 
This pattern indicates that content dominating conscious attention need not dominate dreams, a finding difficult to explain in terms of either classical predictors of incorporation. We propose that existing accounts fail to capture a mechanism that grants certain types of content privileged status as dream material. We introduce Phantom Anxiety Theory, which proposes that the human anxiety system assigns special priority to “safe threats”—objects or events that appear threatening but are remote and require no immediate action. The theory further posits that the anxiety system operates with relative autonomy in monitoring the environment and processing stimuli, including in the selection of dream content.

articles_hidden.title: Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex Causally Supports the Memory Advantage of Reading Aloud
articles_hidden.authors: Lihui Hu; Wenjie Chen; Travis Morgan Seale-Carlisle; Agnieszka Konopka; Manuela Macedonia; Brian Mathias
articles_hidden.abstract: Reading words aloud improves later recognition relative to reading them silently, a phenomenon known as the production effect. This advantage may reflect not only the distinctive sensorimotor information generated by production, but also cognitive control processes that prioritise this information during encoding. Given the central role of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in supporting cognitive control, we tested whether this region causally contributes to the production effect using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In a preregistered within-participant study, 40 adults completed three sessions in which TMS was delivered bilaterally to the DLPFC. They received continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), expected to reduce DLPFC excitability; intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), expected to increase it; or sham stimulation. Participants then read words aloud or silently before completing an old/new recognition test with confidence and recollection judgements. There was a clear production effect: words read aloud were recognised more accurately and quickly, with greater confidence and more frequent recollection ratings, than words read silently. Crucially, cTBS reduced the accuracy advantage for aloud words relative to sham and iTBS. Exploratory receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) and unequal-variance signal-detection (UVSD) modeling approaches provided converging evidence that cTBS reduced the memory advantage for words read aloud. Stimulation did not reliably affect responses to new words. These findings provide the first causal evidence that the DLPFC helps make words read aloud more memorable, consistent with a role for cognitive control in prioritising the distinctive information generated by speaking.

articles_hidden.title: Noradrenaline-centric bias in the pupil-linked arousal literature
articles_hidden.authors: Simon van Gaal; Lola Beerendonk; Haoyue Zhang; Tobias H. Donner; Jan Willem de Gee
articles_hidden.abstract: The literature on pupil-linked arousal shows a pervasive bias: it often attributes findings to the noradrenergic locus coeruleus while overlooking other neuromodulatory systems. Here, we quantify the extent of this bias and emphasize that correcting it is essential for refining theoretical models and improving interpretability in this rapidly evolving field.

articles_hidden.title: How to end a nightmare using ocular distress signaling
articles_hidden.authors: Remington Mallett; Norah Wolk; Daniel Morris; Yasmeen Nahas; Cameron Sandell; Karen Konkoly; Michelle Carr; Ken A. Paller
articles_hidden.abstract: Nightmares trap people in a unique state of helplessness. Whereas fear during wake can be resolved with downregulation strategies, fear during sleep typically coincides with a reduction in the cognitive and social routes to implement them. Here, we report a case in which a dreamer and a technician together overcame both limitations, ending a nightmare in real time. A participant experiencing frequent nightmares was enrolled in a protocol designed to induce lucid dreams (restoring cognition during REM sleep) and enable communication from the dream via eye movements (restoring a social connection). During a nightmare, they gained awareness and used the eye signal as a mayday to request extraction from the dream, all while in polysomnography-verified REM sleep. They were awakened by the technician 34 seconds after the help request and reported immediate relief. At 2- and 4-week follow-ups, lucid dream frequency increased relative to baseline, with lucidity reducing the distress of a subsequent nightmare. Together, these results suggest that real-time dream communication might offer an in somno approach to treating nightmares, a core symptom of PTSD and other psychiatric disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Multidimensional Analysis of Personality Prediction from Electroencephalographic Representations
articles_hidden.authors: Seyed Mahan Mohajerani; Moein Esghaei
articles_hidden.abstract: Associations between personality and resting brain activity have proved difficult to reproduce, leaving unresolved whether electrophysiological information is broadly absent or selectively detectable across personality dimensions. Here, we investigated this question in 254 adults undergoing clinical assessment, examining 15 personality-pattern scales of the Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory–IV using resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We evaluated eight complementary EEG feature families across four representations of personality scores—continuous, two binary thresholds and ordinal—using nested participant-level cross-validation. Most of the 60 scale–formulation combinations showed little predictive performance beyond chance. The strongest evidence concerned Masochistic scores dichotomized at a base-rate score of 60 (area under the curve, 0.630 and 0.594 across two model-aggregation widths), the only combination meeting the within-formulation false-discovery-rate criterion at both widths in fixed-candidate permutation tests. Weaker evidence emerged for continuous Turbulent scores and thresholded Negativistic scores, while an ordinal Histrionic association was identified in a post hoc three-class analysis. Although particular EEG feature families recurred among better-performing configurations, the exact configurations varied across folds. These findings do not support broadly accurate prediction of clinically oriented personality dimensions from resting EEG. Instead, they reveal modest, selective associations whose detection varies across personality dimensions and their operational definitions. Whether these associations generalize, reflect enduring individual differences or provide clinically useful information remains to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Developing human-AI complementarity: Augmenting everyday decision making with Large Language Models
articles_hidden.authors: Adrian Paul Banks; David M Gamblin
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve human judgement, but human–AI systems rarely achieve complementarity: combined performance exceeding that of both humans and AI alone. Across three longitudinal studies (N = 671), we tested whether large language models (LLMs) could support complementarity by contributing to the construction and revision of everyday decision representations. Participants reported real, personally meaningful decisions involving two options and the decision outcome success one week later. As decisions were participant-generated rather than predefined, LLMs dynamically generated considerations and alternative evaluations tailored to each decision. We compared the predictive validity of AI, Human, and augmented evaluations. AI evaluations were standalone LLM predictions of decision outcome success. Human weighted-additive evaluations combined participant-generated attributes, importance weights, and option ratings. Augmented evaluations incorporated LLM-generated attributes and, in later studies, suggested weights and ratings, while participants selected attributes and retained control over evaluations. Augmented evaluations consistently predicted experienced outcomes and showed the strongest observed associations across all three studies. Evidence for complementarity was clearest in Study 2, where fully augmented evaluations outperformed both standalone approaches and explained additional variance in expected and experienced outcomes beyond the standalone evaluations considered together. Across studies, augmentation expanded the attribute set, with participants retaining human and AI contributions. These findings show that human–AI complementarity can emerge in predicting success of real decision outcomes and suggest that decision architecture matters. A distributed cognitive system that integrates AI contributions across all stages of decision making while humans remain responsible for selection and judgement of personally relevant considerations offers a promising architecture for evaluating diverse, personally meaningful real-life decisions.

articles_hidden.title: Reciprocal Relationships between Machiavellianism and Workplace Competition: A Six-Year Longitudinal Study
articles_hidden.authors: XIAOHAN XU; Bart Wille; Louisa Vofrei; Sofie Dupré; Jasmine Vergauwe
articles_hidden.abstract: Machiavellianism is linked to workplace competition, yet it remains unclear whether this association reflects personality-driven activity effects, environment-driven reactivity effects, or a combination of both. This study examined the reciprocal relationships between Machiavellianism and workplace competition across six years of early career development among 1,513 Belgian university graduates. Using both Cross-Lagged Panel Models and Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models, we tested longitudinal activity and reactivity processes at the between-person and within-person levels, respectively. To this end, workplace competition was evaluated using both objective occupational characteristics and subjective perceptions. Regarding activity effects, results showed that higher levels of Machiavellianism at career start positively predicted increases in workplace competition (both objective and subjective), but only at the between-person level of analysis. Additionally, results provided evidence for reactivity effects whereby higher workplace competition predicts increases in Machiavellianism, but only for subjective evaluations of competition and when analyzed at the between-person level. Implications for theory and practice are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: What Drives Leaders to Serve? The Joint and Interactive Effects of HEXACO Personality Traits and Implicit Motives on Servant Leadership
articles_hidden.authors: Justine Amory; Sofie Dupré; J. Malte Runge; Bart Wille
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the channeling hypothesis (Winter et al., 1998), this study examines the role of leaders’ explicit personality traits, implicit motives, and their interaction in predicting servant leadership. Using a dyadic design (N = 219), supervisors completed measures of their HEXACO personality traits and implicit motives, while subordinates rated their servant leadership behavior. Contrary to expectations, neither personality traits nor implicit motives explained unique variance in servant leadership. However, interactions between explicit traits and implicit motives significantly improved prediction. Specifically, leaders high in affiliation motivation were perceived as more servant when they scored high on extraversion and, contrary to expectations, low on agreeableness. These findings highlight the value of considering both implicit motives and explicit traits, as well as their interplay, in understanding servant leadership.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping and Understanding Employees’ Perceived Personality–Work (Mis)Fit: a Mixed-Method Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Sofie Dupré; Jasmine Vergauwe; Bart Wille
articles_hidden.abstract: Although perceived person–environment (P–E) fit has been extensively studied and linked to important workplace outcomes, it has not been examined with the same level of attribute specificity as objective fit. This study addressed that gap by introducing and empirically examining perceived personality–work (mis)fit. Employing a multi-method, multi-informant design with 734 employees and 521 supervisors, we aimed to (a) operationalize perceived personality–work (mis)fit using the too little/too much scale, (b) explore the workplace experiences that shape these perceptions, and (c) examine how they relate to supervisor-rated job performance. We found a high prevalence of perceived misfit, with both deficiency (30%) and excess (42%) commonly reported, while perceived fit was observed across a range of personality trait levels. Thematic analysis revealed that negative experiences associated with perceived misfit extended beyond task performance, encompassing well-being concerns and interpersonal difficulties, with distinct patterns across traits. Finally, perceived personality–work (mis)fit showed modest associations with supervisor-rated job performance. Theoretically, these findings provide insight into how employees experience the fit of their personality at work and highlight the value of examining perceived fit with respect to specific personal attributes. Practically, they inform efforts to better support employees’ fit experiences in the workplace.

articles_hidden.title: Taxing working memory shifts the balance from goals to stimulus-response habits
articles_hidden.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Poppy Watson; Irene van de Vijver; Sanne de Wit
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite our familiarity with the concept of habits, eliciting and measuring habitual “slips of action” experimentally in humans has proven to be difficult. A possible explanation is that participants in psychological experiments actively recruit goal-directed control and therefore make few habitual slips-of-action in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes. In the current experiment we used the symmetrical outcome-revaluation task in combination with a working memory load in an attempt to tip the balance from goal-directed control to stimulus-response habit. During the instrumental learning phase, participants learned to make a Go response to stimuli signalling valuable outcomes (and points) while not responding (NoGo) to stimuli signalling not-valuable outcomes. During the subsequent test phase, the outcomes signalled by the stimuli were either value-congruent with training (still-valuable and still-not-valuable), or value-incongruent (devalued and upvalued). Participants had to flexibly adjust their behaviour on value-incongruent trials where the stimulus-response association learned during training was no longer appropriate. For half the participants, a concurrent working memory load was imposed during the test phase. In line with our preregistered hypotheses, participants showed evidence for habitual slips of action across two experiments, but those under working memory load showed increased habit tendencies (specifically failures to inhibit prepotent Go responses in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes). This central finding suggests that a working memory load can be used to reveal habits in humans.

articles_hidden.title: Supporting Early Career Development Through Volitional Personality Change: A Multi-Layered Evaluation of a Digital Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Sofie Dupré; Bart Wille; Barbara De Clercq; Janne Vanhalst; Joeri Hofmans
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality change interventions (PCIs) offer promising opportunities for personal development, yet little is known about how different psychological layers of personality—thoughts, feelings, behaviors, skills, and identity—respond to intentional change efforts. This study addressed that question through a six-week smartphone-based intervention tailored to students' preparation for entering the workforce, an applied setting in which PCIs remain understudied. Final-year undergraduate clinical psychology students (N = 565) participated in one of three interventions designed to enhance resilience, social boldness, or punctuality, with a quasi-experimental control group for comparison (N = 99). Participants in all three conditions showed meaningful growth in the targeted facet, with gains exceeding changes in non-targeted facets, surpassing those observed in the control group, and persisting at the four-week follow-up. Moreover, perceived feasibility of change moderated intervention effectiveness. Finally, participants targeting resilience and social boldness showed significant growth across psychological layers, whereas those targeting punctuality changed primarily in the behavioral and skill layers. The identity layer—representing how participants see themselves—exhibited the smallest degree of change. Collectively, these findings enrich volitional personality change (VPC) theory by illuminating how personality change unfolds across different psychological layers, while also demonstrating the feasibility of PCIs in supporting the school-to-work transition.

articles_hidden.title: PsyScale Studio: A Guided, Browser-Based Application for Developing and Validating Measurement Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Assis Kamu; Nicholas Tze Ping Pang; Ho Chong Mun
articles_hidden.abstract: Validating a measurement scale requires a long sequence of analyses, from content validity and item analysis to factor analysis, item response theory, fairness and relations to other variables. These analyses are spread across several programs, and many applied researchers find them difficult to choose, run and report. PsyScale Studio is a free web application that guides users through this sequence. Users describe their study purpose and response format (ten formats, from dichotomous tests to forced-choice and formative indices); the application then builds a purpose-specific roadmap, runs each analysis and explains every result in English or Malay with criteria, references and reporting text. Classical, exploratory and Rasch analyses run in JavaScript. Confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance, polytomous item response theory, differential item functioning and cognitive diagnostic models run in R compiled to WebAssembly (webR), using lavaan, semTools, mirt and CDM, while the data stay on the user’s computer. Outputs include an APA-style Word report with references and a reproducibility package with the exact R code and input of each analysis. All 12 comparisons of the JavaScript engine with R (psych, eRm) were within tolerance, and the application’s confirmatory factor analysis reproduced lavaan to four decimals. A simulated 21-item mental health scale with known properties illustrates the workflow; the application recovered its factor structure, weak item and differential item functioning. A second example applies cognitive diagnostic models to Tatsuoka’s fraction-subtraction data. PsyScale Studio is available at https://psyscale-studio.web.app.

articles_hidden.title: The Dutch Gambling Harms Question Inventory (D-GHQI-12): 	 Development, psychometric properties and test-retest reliability
articles_hidden.authors: Suzanne Geurts; Heather Wardle; Ruth van Holst; Mijntje Meijer; Antonius J. Van Rooij
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction. The Netherlands lacks a standardized Dutch-language questionnaire to measure gambling harms. To address this, the current study aimed to develop and validate a set of questions spanning all gambling harms domains relevant to the Dutch context drawing on existing questionnaires. 

Method. First, the performance of 26 newly developed and translated items, covering eight harm domains, was evaluated. The convergent validity, test-retest stability and adequate content coverage of the item pool were evaluated. Beyond gambling product use and engagement, reference points included the Problem Gambling Severity Index, CBA-MI Reported Financial Wellbeing Scale, Australian Personal Wellbeing scale, and Mental Health Inventory (MHI-5). Secondly, the best performing items were selected for a short form scale, to support a high chance of adoption in monitoring. 

Results. Items performed well across multiple psychometric criteria. They demonstrated high levels of understandability, generally supportive evidence for convergent validity, and satisfactory temporal stability. These items also correlated in expected ways with participation in higher risk gambling products. Based on these results, a choice of the most suitable item from each harm domain was made, to construct the Dutch Gambling Harms Question Inventory (D-GHQI-12). 

Conclusion. The new 12 item Dutch gambling harms scale was constructed around explicit harm domains, verified with international experts and Dutch stakeholders, including those with lived experience of gambling harms. This ensured that most recognised domains, including crime, physical health, mental health, and financial harms, are represented by at least one item in the inventory. Taken together, the D-GHQI-12 offers a domain-balanced, Dutch-validated tool for population monitoring.

articles_hidden.title: Inference-Time Self-Guidance for Conversational Safety in Delusion-Related Interactions
articles_hidden.authors: David Piterman; Elad Refoua; Hadar Dery; Gunther Meinlschmidt; Ziv Ben-Zion; Kfir Bar; Zohar Elyoseph
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in psychologically sensitive conversations, where repeated affirmation may reinforce delusion-related beliefs and associated risk. Inference-time self-guidance, in which a model generates conversation-specific guidance for subsequent responses without parameter updates, may offer an approach to conversational safety, but its utility in delusion-related interactions remains unclear.
Objective: To develop and evaluate conversation-specific inference-time self-guidance for conversational safety in delusion-related interactions.
Methods: In this preregistered study, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and DeepSeek V4 Flash completed 16 Psychosis-Bench scenarios under Baseline and three self-guidance conditions: response rules, contrastive examples, and short-horizon consequence simulation. The fully crossed design yielded 192 conversations and 2,304 assistant turns. A separate automated judge scored Delusion Confirmation (DCS), Harm Enablement (HES), and Safety Intervention (SIS) using published Psychosis-Bench rubrics. Analyses compared benchmark-defined Explicit and Implicit risk-cue scenarios and examined whether self-guidance reduced this gap.
Results: Across models, all three self-guidance conditions significantly reduced delusion confirmation and harm enablement and increased safety intervention relative to Baseline (all nine PFDR<.001; dz = 1.10–2.17). At Baseline, explicit risk cues elicited significantly greater SIS than matched implicit cues, whereas cue-type differences in DCS and HES were not significant. Self-guidance did not significantly attenuate the explicit–implicit safety gap after correction for multiple comparisons.
Conclusions: Model-generated inference-time self-guidance improved benchmark-defined safety behavior during standardized scripted escalation without parameter updates. These findings support further evaluation of inference-time self-guidance for delusion-related conversational safety, particularly when risk is communicated indirectly.

articles_hidden.title: Peers link conflict-resolution reputation to social and cognitive capacities rather than the capacity to impose costs among Ethiopian forager-horticulturalists
articles_hidden.authors: Zachary H Garfield; Erik Ringen; Edward H Hagen
articles_hidden.abstract: Leadership emergence in socially egalitarian contexts depends on the qualities of individuals and on how others perceive their capacity to use them. Multi-Capital Leadership theory proposes that leaders deploy material, social, somatic, and neural capital to solve problems of group living by providing benefits to group members or imposing costs. Conflict resolution is one important leadership domain. We reanalyse peer rankings of 60 adults in a relatively egalitarian community of Chabu forager-horticulturalists in southwest Ethiopia. Seven peer-raters ranked participants on twelve traits identified as relevant to leadership in contemporary evolutionary theories. A previous analysis averaged rankings before modelling, obscuring differences among raters and treating positions within an ordering as continuous measurements. Here, we fitted a multivariate Plackett–Luce model directly to the individual rankings. This accounts for dependence within rankings and incorporates uncertainty into estimates. It also allows us to estimate consensus orderings and systematic variation associated with rater sex. Male and female peer-raters produced broadly similar orderings, including for conflict resolution. This could reflect actual covariation in participants’ qualities, a shared evaluative schema, or both. Peer-ranked proxies for material, social, and neural capital covaried closely and did not form clearly separable perceptual domains. The clearest descriptive contrast was between benefit-related attributes, including conflict resolution, sound decision-making, and prosociality, and cost-related attributes, including being feared and fighting. Conflict-resolution reputation was most closely associated with decision-making, kin support, respect, and intelligence, and showed no clear positive association with fighting. In these rankings, a reputation for conflict resolution was more clearly distinguished from aggression and coercion than were measures capturing the three capital domains represented in the instrument.

articles_hidden.title: The Cognitive Science of Maria Montessori.
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Desirée Di Paolo
articles_hidden.abstract: Maria Montessori is among the most globally influential figures in the history of education, yet she remains almost entirely absent from the history of science. This paper argues that her absence is unwarranted, and that her work is best understood not as pedagogy but as the empirical investigation of cognitive development by a scientist trained in the positivist and evolutionary milieu of late nineteenth-century Rome. Drawing on Italian-language sources and untranslated early publications, we reconstruct her scientific formation, in particular her relationships with the anthropologist Giuseppe Sergi and the experimental psychologist Sante De Sanctis. We believe that these relationships gave her a theory of cognitive development structured around three irreducible and simultaneous dimensions: individual variation, the designed material environment, and the socio-cultural context. The prepared environment, the central contribution of her method, was designed to make these dimensions explicit and tractable, and maps with notable precision onto frameworks that cognitive science has formalised only recently. We then ask why this scientific dimension of her work has gone so consistently unseen, identifying three historical and contingent causes: a communicative style bent by financial and political necessity, systematic losses in translation, and the structural exclusion she faced as a woman in the scientific institutions of her time. We close with the case of Jean Piaget, whose sustained exposure to Montessori's method, and subsequent formalisation of a developmental theory that diverged from hers on precisely the points where later research has moved back in her direction, offers the sharpest illustration of what the misreading has cost.

articles_hidden.title: Visual Properties of E-Mobility Devices Shape Their On-Road Vulnerability: Effects of Size and Speed
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Wang; Madeline Jarvis; Ella Du Plessis; Ariella Stephen; Blake Jones; Narelle Haworth; Hinze Hogendoorn
articles_hidden.abstract: The brief visual window—often only hundreds of milliseconds—in which drivers predict the arrival of oncoming vehicles and decide whether to give way is critical for safe and efficient manoeuvring. E-mobility devices (EMDs) are a relatively new form of transportation and may challenge these decisions due to their small visual profile and relatively high operating speeds. Here, we examined whether observers show systematic biases when judging EMDs relative to other common vehicles, potentially contributing to their vulnerability in intersection crashes. Using naturalistic video stimuli spanning seven vehicle categories, we tested whether observers would overestimate the time-to-arrival (TTA) of EMDs and, consequently, accept smaller gaps for them to pass through an intersection. Consistent with this prediction, EMDs elicited greater biases in both TTA and gap judgements (N = 31 and N = 59), with these effects further amplified on a visually complex road. By comparing across vehicle categories under naturalistic viewing conditions, the results provide evidence that the amplified biases observed for EMDs arise from differences in the underlying visual signals available to observers—specifically, their smaller retinal size and potentially less reliable motion cues at higher speeds. Importantly, these biases were not explained by speed misperception: in a separate two-alternative forced-choice task (N = 49), EMDs were perceived as faster, not slower, than other vehicles at matched speeds. This dissociation indicates that TTA overestimation cannot be attributed to speed underestimation alone. Together, these findings link controlled psychophysical processes to real-world traffic behaviour, with implications for future experimental design and traffic safety policy.

articles_hidden.title: The case for a developmentally-informed education system in the early years
articles_hidden.authors: Jenny Louise Gibson; Sally Hogg
articles_hidden.abstract: A developmentally-informed early years system is one that is underpinned by a clear understanding of children. In this chapter we argue that this involves integrating scientific insights into child development with expertise in how public policy, services and practices can influence this development. We present a framework of six core principles capturing essential knowledge about child development, which we propose should inform decisions about early childhood education and associated policies and services. We explore these principles in the context of the Early Years landscape in England. We consider challenges for this framework in the current system and explore what might be done to make the whole system – from front line practice to national policy – more developmentally- informed.

articles_hidden.title: Reconfiguration of parental defense by offspring presence in humans
articles_hidden.authors: Joana Vieira; Matteo Sequestro; Simon Lindhagen; Kristjan Suuder; Andreas Olsson
articles_hidden.abstract: Offspring survival depends on parental behavior, both for providing immediate protection from danger, and for transmitting information about what is dangerous and how best to avoid it. In rodents, the presence of offspring changes parental responses to danger, facilitating active threat coping over freezing. We investigated whether offspring presence reshapes human parental defense in a similar way, and whether parental defense in turn affects how effectively children learn vicariously about threats. We developed a virtual reality-based naturalistic paradigm where parents were able to display unconstrained defensive responses to a virtual attacker. Eighty-five parents participated with their own child, and forty with an unrelated child. All parents performed the task twice, once alone and once in the presence of the own/unrelated child. With their own child relative to alone, parents showed reduced freezing-like behavior, fought the attacker faster and more precisely, and stayed closer to their child. In turn, children sharing the environment with their parent showed enhanced physiological differentiation of sound cues predicting threat or safety. Moreover, increased proximity to the parent (but not to an unrelated adult) enhanced attack expectancy reported by the child afterwards. Altogether, our findings parallel and extend prior reports in rodents, and suggest that offspring presence induces an evolutionarily conserved reorganization of parental defense that facilitates both offspring protection and transmission of threat information.

articles_hidden.title: A systematic review of implicit statistical learning in schizophrenia spectrum disorders
articles_hidden.authors: karolina.knizkova@nudz.cz; Monika Vecerova; Kateřina Horníková; Mabel Rodriguez; Barbora Kerkova
articles_hidden.abstract: This systematic review examined current findings on implicit statistical learning (ISL) in schizophrenia spectrum disorders and the factors that influence performance. We aimed to update and expand the existing literature by including various ISL tasks, such as serial reaction time, artificial grammar learning, or transitional probabilities. We also considered several ISL moderators related to the characteristics of these tasks, as well as a host of potential clinical and cognitive correlates. We searched PubMed, Scopus, PsycINFO, and MEDLINE Complete for original studies published in English involving adults diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Twenty-one studies published between 1992 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. We extracted relevant data including study information and design, sample characteristics, ISL task type and characteristics, and main outcomes. Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Assessment Scale. Findings were heterogeneous, with studies reporting both intact and impaired ISL. The most frequently reported outcome with the largest aggregate patient sample showed that ISL was preserved in comparison to healthy controls. Seven studies reported ISL deficits, and the rest reported mixed or condition-specific findings. The most promising moderators included task and stimulus type. Disorganized symptomatology and working memory span consistently correlated with ISL performance. In contrast, antipsychotic dosage, overall symptomatology, illness duration, or explicit memory did not show consistent associations with ISL.

articles_hidden.title: Gaming disorder assessment tools: A comprehensive systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Muddsar Hameed; Matthew Stevens; Marcela Radunz; Christina R. Galanis; Sanni Behm; Henrietta Bowden-Jones; Joel Billieux; Simone Rodda; Stéphanie Baggio; Katajun Lindenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Gaming disorder (GD) is an emerging addictive disorder, comparable to gambling disorder, that has been included in the International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision (ICD-11). Globally, the study of GD has grown rapidly but the research base has been criticized for its inconsistent assessment. This comprehensive systematic review aimed to update two previous reviews (2013, 2020) to evaluate all English-language GD tools and their research evidence. A database search identified 49 tools employed across 1,296 peer-reviewed studies involving more than 2.7 million participants. Tools were evaluated according to: conceptual alignment and practical utility; compatibility with DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 criteria; sample and study characteristics; and psychometric properties. The evaluation showed that the GD field has greatly proliferated across its health subdisciplines and quadrupled in size since 2020. Based on review data from 2013 and 2020, and assuming similar growth and sustainability, the GD field may increase to more than 2,000 studies by 2033. Key findings included: (1) tool coverage of DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 criteria has improved, particularly for assessment of impaired control; (2) instrument choice differs considerably across epidemiological, neurobiological, and treatment research streams; and (3) many tools demonstrate basic reliability and validity indicators, but more rigorous psychometric validation is needed. The GD field would benefit from an international ‘gold standard’ tool to harmonize measurement and generate a more cohesive evidence base. To advance, the field should capitalize on opportunities for innovation in screening to more effectively assess the unique needs, challenges, and characteristics of gaming populations.

articles_hidden.title: Excitation-inhibition imbalance in depression and the limits of observability: cohort-level inference from resting-state EEG with an amortised three-region Wilson-Cowan model
articles_hidden.authors: peng yu; ze yang; Shiqi Zhang; Cui Ruolin; Liu Yijun; cheng kang; lu cao; ning ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression is widely thought to involve an imbalance between neuronal excitation and inhibition, but the idea has rarely been tested quantitatively at the level of macroscopic brain networks, because dynamical models are hard to fit to EEG spectra and fitting them person by person is prohibitively slow. We present a complete, reproducible pipeline that makes such a test possible, and we report where it succeeds and where it does not. Using eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants (22 with lifetime major depressive disorder, 95 without), we fitted a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model with an amortised Bayesian method, in which a single shared library of simulations serves every participant and reduces inference to milliseconds per person. Depressed participants showed a consistent shift towards excitation in three core networks, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive. The model's default-mode resonance frequency rose with symptom severity, whereas the conventional peak-frequency estimate computed from the same recordings did not. We then asked what the model actually buys. For distinguishing groups it did not outperform simple spectral measures, and its per-person low-frequency predictions were poor, so we restrict our claims accordingly. A real-time state observer detected sudden shifts in the network's operating point within milliseconds, yet could not reconstruct the moment-to-moment state, a limit set by the model's intrinsic randomness rather than by our algorithm. Finally, a dose-matched control showed that closed-loop stimulation is no more accurate than a fixed stimulus at the same dose, so we report the real-time feasibility of the loop without claiming an accuracy advantage. The contribution of the paper is therefore a reusable, calibrated inference pipeline together with an explicit map of its limits, including negative findings that we deliberately kept as results.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in vision science: The case for a paradigm shift, what it buys, and how to do it well
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Nearly a decade ago, Mollon, Bosten, Peterzell, and Webster (2017) asked what individual differences can teach visual science and what counts as good experimental practice. Studies since then have changed both answers. The study of individual differences is a paradigm, not a technique, with its own objects, standards of evidence, and products. Long practiced in the shadows by a small group, it should move into the mainstream and integrate with existing paradigms, treating differences among observers as evidence rather than error. Its central object is the latent factor, which can earn roles from latent mechanism to established mechanism, computational phenotype, heritable phenotype, endophenotype, or factor-targeted marker, each requiring stricter evidence. Twelve pillars organize what the paradigm buys, including links across domains and levels and tests of whether constructs are unitary. Several 2017 conclusions need correction, above all the definition of true individual differences as stable, long-term traits, and the 2017 prescriptions (rank statistics, required test-retest reliability, fixed test order, mandatory blocking, blanket correction for multiple comparisons) each trade one error for another. Because global artifacts produce general factors, tuned factor structure is itself evidence against them. The long-term goal is a computational atlas of human visual variation: its mechanisms, their sources, and optimal markers for the clinic and for design.

articles_hidden.title: Psychophysiological correlates of fear of movement-related pain assessed during a picture-based paradigm in people with chronic shoulder pain
articles_hidden.authors: Larissa Pagels; Niklas Fengler; Ann Meulders; Waclaw M. Adamczyk; Frédéric Li; Falco Lentzsch; habil. Marcin Grzegorzek; Marcela Camargo Tozzo; Anamaria Siriani de Oliveira; Kerstin Luedtke
articles_hidden.abstract: Fear of movement-related pain (FMRP) contributes to disability in chronic musculoskeletal pain. However, psychophysiological correlates of activity-specific threat appraisal during FMRP-eliciting tasks remain insufficiently understood. This cross-sectional study examined self-reports and psycho-physiological responses to shoulder-straining daily activities in individuals with chronic shoulder pain (CSP) and pain-free controls. Participants observed six pictures depicting shoulder movements select-ed as highly or minimally threatening. Each picture was presented five times in random order. Partic-ipants were informed that they would subsequently perform the activities. Following each presenta-tion, participants rated anticipated fear, urge to avoid, and expected harmfulness. Electrodermal ac-tivity, pupil diameter, heart rate, respiratory rate, and gaze behavior were recorded continuously. Self-reports differentiated between highly and minimally threatening activities and were higher in the CSP group (p≤0.001). SCL differentiated between threat categories, with more pronounced responses in the CSP group (pBH-corrected=0.008; f2=0.029). Within the CSP group, SCL correlated weakly with ratings of fear (ρ=0.137; pBH-corrected=0.008) and harmfulness (ρ=0.127; pBH-corrected=0.013), but not urge to avoid (ρ=0.022; pBH-corrected=0.763). Pupil dilation (pBH-corrected≤0.001; f2=0.039) and gaze be-havior (pBH-corrected=0.006; f2=0.067) differed between individual pictures in the CSP group but did not consistently differentiate the predefined threat categories. Heart rate and respiratory rate showed no consistent effects. This is the first shoulder-specific picture-viewing paradigm combining self-reports with several psychophysiological measures and the first study to examine pupil dilation as a potential correlate of FMRP. The findings suggest that electrodermal activity may reflect sympathetic arousal related to activity-specific threat appraisal during FMRP-eliciting picture-viewing.

articles_hidden.title: The Cost of Disconnection: Longitudinal Egocentric Network Analyses Linking Social Isolation to Loneliness and Mental Health in Adolescents and Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Lu Zhang; Alba Bruggeman Nelissen; Sarah Daniels; Matthew Richards; Jack L Andrews; Susanne Schweizer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Social disconnection has been proposed as a contributing factor to the youth mental health crisis. However, it remains unclear how social disruptions reshape social networks and their links to mental wellbeing across age groups. The present study examined whether social disruptions (during the COVID-19 pandemic) reshape social networks and how changes in social networks differently relate to mental health and loneliness in adolescents compared to adults. 
Methods: The study used egocentric network analysis of data from 1,278 participants (88% female; aged 11-89 years, mean = 37.2±16.2 years) in the multinational (Australia, the U.K., and U.S.) prospective COVID-19 Risks Across the Lifespan (CORAL) Study. Social network properties of structural density, functional closeness, and interaction frequency were derived. Linear mixed-effects modelling was employed to examine cross-sectional and prospective associations with mental wellbeing at baseline, three-month, and six-month follow-up.
Results: Adolescents reported more virtual interactions, and less in-person contact. Greater network closeness was associated with lower depression, whereas dense but less close networks were linked to greater loneliness. Reduced contact from pre-pandemic levels were also linked to poorer wellbeing, particularly among younger individuals. 
Conclusions: The present findings highlight that age differences in social experiences, such as social network structure (density) and function (closeness and interaction frequency), may underlie young people’s greater mental health vulnerability during social disruptions. This underscores the importance of developing age-sensitive and context-responsive strategies to better support mental wellbeing during times of social disruption.

articles_hidden.title: Does creative engagement spill over to calculated risk taking?
articles_hidden.authors: Shenghui Xiaoyong; Zhuoqi Yin; Huimin Kong; Kelong Lu
articles_hidden.abstract: Creative engagement may shape not only the ideas people generate but also their willingness to take calculated risks in subsequent decisions, yet this possibility remains underexplored. Across three studies, we examined this relationship and whether general self-efficacy or affective state accounts for the relationship. Study 1 (N = 228) used a cross-sectional survey and found that everyday creative ideation behavior was positively associated with overall and domain-specific risk-taking propensity. General self-efficacy did not mediate this association. Study 2 (N = 83) experimentally compared calculated risk taking after creative drawing versus standard coloring using a binary lottery choice. Creative drawing increased affective dominance but did not significantly influence calculated risk taking. Study 3 (N = 94) compared calculated risk taking after creative writing versus standard typing using a six-level investment-choice task. Creative writing increased both calculated risk taking and affective dominance, but the change in dominance did not mediate the effect on calculated risk taking. These findings suggest that creative engagement can influence subsequent calculated risk taking, although the effect may depend on the creative task and the sensitivity of the risk measure. Neither general self-efficacy nor affective dominance explained this relationship, highlighting the need to investigate alternative psychological mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: “I shape my world around my sensitivities”: Auditory environments and sound sensitivity in intermittently-/non-speaking autistic adults
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Poulsen; Ari Angel Star-McKenzie; Tim Chan; Melanie Heyworth; Liz Pellicano; Diana Weiting Tan
articles_hidden.abstract: Auditory environments shape autistic people’s everyday experiences and quality of life (QoL). However, existing literature tends to characterize these experiences primarily as ‘hypersensitivity’, lacking nuance in how everyday auditory environments shape lived experience. Studies focusing on the experiences of autistic people who are intermittently-/non-speaking are also scarce. This study examined auditory experiences in the presence or absence of competing background noise, operationalized through noisy and quiet everyday environments, among intermittently-/non-speaking and speaking autistic adults. 419 autistic adults (Mage=32.2 yrs, SDage=11.3) completed an online survey including a bespoke questionnaire on everyday sound experiences and a sound-related QoL measure. Of these participants, 383 (91%) predominantly used speech while 36 (9%) were intermittently-/non-speaking. Open-text responses from intermittently-/non-speaking participants were analyzed using content analysis. Statistical analyses revealed that intermittently-/non-speaking participants reported greater sound-related impacts on QoL, greater difficulty in quiet environments, and elevated pain hyperacusis compared with speaking participants. Content analysis contextualized these findings: participants often sought predictable environments to support regulation. Adaptive strategies, including selective withdrawal, preparation, and environmental modification, were framed as proactive self-regulation. Together, the findings position sensory accessibility as an environmental design consideration rather than an individual burden, while centering autonomy in managing auditory input to foster inclusion and wellbeing.

articles_hidden.title: The Feasibility of Conducting Research on Cannabis Use in Early Adolescents in England
articles_hidden.authors: Yifan Huang; Leah Fawaz; Amanda Sarpong; Shareha Saiady; Chloe Dagcevizi; Solveig Carer; Kelly Charge; Maria Livanou; Jake Camp; Amy Lineham
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Approximately 10% of early adolescents in the UK report lifetime cannabis use. However, contemporary UK research in this population remains limited due to recruitment, consent and safeguarding challenges. We explored the feasibility of conducting research about cannabis use in UK adolescents aged 13–15 years.

Methods: This exploratory feasibility project comprised an online quantitative survey and qualitative interviews on cannabis use and mental health. Participants aged 13-15 years were recruited through schools, drug services, social media, posters and word-of-mouth. Participants consented through either a standard parent-and-adolescent pathway or an independent Gillick-competent pathway. Feasibility outcomes included total recruitment, cannabis-user recruitment, successful data collection, and the extent of safeguarding actions required. 

Results: 175 participants completed the survey (Mage = 14.35, 54.9% female) and n=13 (7.4%) reported lifetime cannabis use. 16 participants (Mage=14.56, 75.0% female) completed the qualitative interview study, including 11 lifetime cannabis users. Two and four cannabis-using participants used the Gillick-competent pathway in the quantitative and qualitative studies, respectively. In the quantitative study, 38/175 participants (21.7%) triggered low-intensity signposting and one participant received additional safeguarding actions. Three qualitative participants received safeguarding actions. Both studies successfully elicited detailed information on cannabis use, mental health and contextual experiences.

Conclusion: We recruited nearly 200 13-15-year-old adolescent participants, including those who used cannabis, collected rich data about illegal cannabis use and mental health using in-depth surveys and interviews, while keeping participants safe. We therefore proved we can feasibly conduct research about cannabis in <16-year-olds in the UK.

articles_hidden.title: Tracking the Integration of Novel Words into the Mental Lexicon: Evidence from Mouse Movement Trajectories
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew P. Lucas; Richard J. O'Connor; Kevin J. Riggs; Shane Lindsay
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated lexical competition effects in novel word learning using mouse tracking methodology. We conducted two experiments examining how and when novel word representations become lexicalised, focusing on their ability to engage in competition with existing lexical entries. In Experiment 1, we used mouse tracking to conceptually replicate Weighall et al.’s (2017) eye tracking study, examining lexical competition between newly learnt word–referent pairs and familiar words both immediately after learning and following overnight consolidation.
